documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Fractions · maths · GCSE Mathematics, number: fractions · Key Stage 3 to Foundation GCSE · version 1.1.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Decide which of two fractions is larger and justify it by the size of the pieces, not the size of the numbers. · You will show this by: Given three eighths and two fifths, the learner writes that three eighths is smaller because fifteen fortieths is fewer than sixteen fortieths — or compares each with one half — rather than because eight is bigger than four. · Write an equivalent fraction and explain why its value has not changed. · You will show this by: The learner produces fifteen twentieths for three quarters and says that multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number renames the pieces without changing how much there is. · Place a fraction on a number line between zero and one and read its position as a size. · You will show this by: The learner puts five eighths to the right of one half and left of one, and says why it is nearer to one half than to one. · Before you start · A chocolate bar is cut into four equal pieces and you eat one. A second identical bar is cut into eight equal pieces and you eat one of those. Which piece was bigger, and why? · What does twelve divided by three mean, in words? · Why this matters · Two friends order the same size pizza. One cuts hers into four slices and eats one. The other cuts his into eight slices and eats one. Both say they had a slice, and one of them had twice as much pizza as the other. · Both statements are true, and the reason is the whole idea: a fraction is two numbers doing two different jobs. The bottom number says how many pieces the whole was cut into — it is a size. The top number counts the pieces you have — it is an amount. Almost every fraction mistake comes from reading the bottom number as though it were the top one. · The explanation · Fractions count pieces of a declared size · In three quarters, the four declares that the whole was cut into four equal pieces, and the three says how many of them you have. Read it aloud that way — three pieces, each a quarter — and the notation stops being two numbers stacked on top of each other. The bar between them is not a minus sign and not a division you have forgotten to finish; it is the word of, as in three of the four equal pieces. · That reading immediately explains the fact that surprises almost everyone: one eighth is smaller than one quarter, even though eight is bigger than four. The bottom number is not how much you get. It is how many ways the whole was divided, so a larger bottom number means a smaller slice. If you cut the same cake into more pieces, each piece must be smaller — there is no way around it, because the cake did not grow. · The same amount can wear different names · One half, two quarters and three sixths are the same amount of the same whole. Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number doubles the count and halves the piece size at the same time, and those two changes cancel exactly. You are renaming the pieces, not changing the amount of cake. That is why an equivalent fraction is written with an equals sign rather than an arrow: the number has not moved. · This is the move that makes comparison possible. Two fractions cut into different sizes of piece cannot be compared by their top numbers, because three big pieces and two small pieces are not counts of the same thing. Give both fractions the same denominator — the same size of piece — and the top numbers become plain counts that can be compared directly. · A fraction is one number in a place on the line · Three quarters is not a calculation waiting to happen. It is a single number that sits between zero and one, closer to one than to zero. Once you can see it there, adding, comparing and scaling it are operations on a number rather than rules about two integers that happen to be written above and below a line. · The number line also gives you a check that needs no arithmetic at all. Compare each fraction with one half: a fraction whose top is less than half its bottom is below one half, and one whose top is more than half its bottom is above it. Three eighths is below one half because three is less than four; two fifths is below one half because two is less than two and a half. To decide between them you still need a common denominator, but the check tells you immediately when an answer is impossible. · Decimals and percentages are the same number in another notation · Three quarters is also nought point seven five and also seventy-five per cent. Nothing about the quantity changes when the notation does: a fraction, a decimal and a percentage are three ways of writing one position on the number line. A learner who knows where three quarters sits already knows most of what the next two topics teach, and a learner who does not will find percentages mysterious for a reason that has nothing to do with percentages. · Diagrams and representations · The same amount written three ways. Each line is one number, not a sum. · 3/4 = 0.75 = 75% · Three quarters, nought point seven five and seventy-five per cent are the same position on the number line. The equals signs are true because the quantity is unchanged, only its name. · Two identical bars. The top bar is cut into four equal parts with three shaded; the bottom is cut into eight equal parts with six shaded. The shaded area is the same, which is what three quarters equals six eighths means. · bar A: 4 parts, 3 shaded | bar B: 8 parts, 6 shaded · Cutting every quarter in half doubles the number of pieces and halves each piece, so the shaded amount does not move. This is why multiplying top and bottom by the same number never changes the value. · A line from zero to one with halves marked, then quarters, then eighths. Three quarters sits three quarters of the way along; five eighths sits just past the halfway mark. · 0 — 1/8 — 1/4 — 3/8 — 1/2 — 5/8 — 3/4 — 7/8 — 1 · Position is size. Five eighths is past one half because five is more than half of eight, and that comparison needs no common denominator. · Worked examples · Which is larger, three eighths or two fifths? Show how you decide. · Notice that the two fractions are cut into different sizes of piece: eighths and fifths, so the top numbers cannot be compared yet. · Why: Comparing three with two only works when both counts describe pieces of the same size. Here three eighths and two fifths are counts of different things. · Rewrite both with a common denominator of forty: three eighths becomes fifteen fortieths, and two fifths becomes sixteen fortieths. · Why: Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number renames the pieces without changing the amount, so each fraction keeps its value. Forty is the smallest number that both eight and five divide into. · Now compare the counts of fortieths: fifteen is fewer than sixteen, so three eighths is the smaller fraction. · Why: Once the pieces are the same size, the top number is a plain count and can be compared directly. Fifteen fortieths is less than sixteen fortieths. · Answer: three eighths is smaller than two fifths (15/40 against 16/40, so 3/8 < 2/5) · One recipe uses three quarters of a bag of flour and another uses five sixths of a bag. Which uses more, and by what fraction of a bag? · Find a common denominator for quarters and sixths, which is twelve. · Why: The two amounts are in different sizes of piece, so they cannot be subtracted or compared until the pieces match. Twelve is the smallest number both four and six divide into. · Convert both: three quarters is nine twelfths, and five sixths is ten twelfths. · Why: Each conversion multiplies top and bottom by the same number, so the amount of flour in each recipe is unchanged — only the way it is counted changes. · Compare ten twelfths with nine twelfths, then subtract to find the difference: ten minus nine is one twelfth. · Why: With equal-sized pieces the counts can be compared and subtracted directly. The answer is a difference of one twelfth of a bag, not one twelfth of a recipe. · Answer: five sixths is larger, by 1/12 of a bag · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: One eighth is bigger than one quarter, because eight is bigger than four. · Why it fails: The bottom number counts the pieces, so a larger bottom number means each piece is smaller. Cutting the same bar into eight makes every piece half the size of the quarter you had before. The numbers on the bottom are describing the cut, not the amount. · Correct reasoning: Read the bottom number as a size and the top as a count. One piece of a bar cut into eight is smaller than one piece of the same bar cut into four, because there are more pieces sharing the same whole. · Wrong: 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4 · Right: 1/8 < 1/4 because eighths are half the size of quarters · Wrong belief: Two fractions with different bottom numbers can be compared by looking at their top numbers. · Why it fails: The top number is a count of pieces, and a piece of one size is not the same as a piece of another. Two large slices and three small slices cannot be counted against each other until the slices are the same size. Comparing tops alone answers a different question from the one that was asked. · Correct reasoning: Make the pieces the same size first, by finding a common denominator, and only then compare the counts. Alternatively compare each fraction with one half, which needs no conversion. · Wrong: 3/8 > 2/5 because 3 > 2 · Right: 3/8 < 2/5 because 15/40 < 16/40 · Wrong belief: Adding two fractions means adding the tops and adding the bottoms. · Why it fails: Adding the bottoms changes the size of every piece in the answer, so the sum is no longer made of the pieces you started with. One half plus one half would become two quarters, which is one half — but two halves are a whole. The arithmetic has described a different operation from the one intended. · Correct reasoning: Add counts of pieces that are already the same size. If the denominators match, add only the tops. If they do not, convert to a common denominator first, then add the tops. · Wrong: 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/4 · Right: 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/2 = 1 · Guided practice · Which is larger, two thirds or three fifths? Show the common denominator you used. · Hint: The smallest number that both three and five divide into is fifteen. Convert both fractions to fifteenths before comparing. · Write a fraction equivalent to three quarters with denominator twenty. · Hint: Ask what four was multiplied by to reach twenty, then multiply the top by the same number. · Put five eighths, one half and nine sixteenths in order, smallest first. · Hint: Sixteenths is a common denominator for all three. Convert each fraction before ordering. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 16 marks. · Explain why one eighth is smaller than one quarter, even though eight is larger than four. · 4 marks · Sam writes one half plus one half equals two quarters. Explain what has gone wrong and give the correct answer. · 4 marks · The bar is split into four equal parts and three of them are shaded. Match each description to the position on the drawing it describes. · 4 marks · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · A rectangle divided into four equal vertical sections. The left three sections are shaded and the right section is unshaded. Numbered positions mark one shaded section, the unshaded section, the whole bar and the bar's lower edge. · Labels: A. The denominator: the whole cut into four equal parts · B. The numerator: the number of shaded quarters · C. The part that is not shaded, also one quarter · D. One equal part, which is one quarter of the bar · Write the letter of the correct label beside each numbered position. · 1. ____________ · 2. ____________ · 3. ____________ · 4. ____________ · Work out one half plus one quarter. Give your answer as a fraction. · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · Two classes of the same size sit the same test. Three fifths of Class A pass and five eighths of Class B pass. Which class had the larger share pass? Decide without turning either fraction into a percentage, and say how you know. · The comparison is the same one the worked example made, but the familiar bar model is gone and the quantities are described as shares of a group rather than parts of a shape. The learner has to choose the method rather than follow a diagram. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Without a calculator, say which is larger: seven twelfths or four sevenths. (next day) · Write nought point six as a fraction in its simplest form, and explain the link to tenths. (week later) · A learner says one ninth is bigger than one tenth because nine is bigger than ten. What would you say to them? (month later) · Summary · The bottom number names the size of the pieces; the top number counts them. · More pieces means smaller pieces, so a larger denominator is a smaller fraction. · Multiplying top and bottom by the same number renames the pieces without changing the amount, which is what makes comparison possible. · A fraction is one number at one place on the line — decimals and percentages are the same place in another notation. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Quadratic equations · maths · GCSE Mathematics, algebra: quadratic equations and graphs · Key Stage 4, Foundation to Higher · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Solve a quadratic equation by factorising, and explain why a product equal to zero lets you split the equation into two simpler equations. · You will show this by: Given x squared plus five x plus six equals zero, the learner writes the two factors, sets each factor to zero, and explains that a product can be zero only when at least one factor is zero. · Decide whether a quadratic has two, one or no real solutions by using the discriminant, and connect that number to the graph. · You will show this by: For x squared minus four x plus five equals zero, the learner calculates the discriminant as negative four, states that there are no real roots, and says the parabola does not cross the x-axis. · Translate a geometric or everyday situation into a quadratic and reject a solution that the situation cannot allow. · You will show this by: For a rectangle whose length is five centimetres more than its width and whose area is twenty-four square centimetres, the learner forms x times x plus five equals twenty-four, solves it, and rejects the negative root because a length cannot be negative. · Before you start · Expand (x + 2)(x + 3). · What does the graph of y equals x squared look like, and where does it cross the x-axis? · Why this matters · A rectangular garden is five metres longer than it is wide, and its area is twenty-four square metres. You could guess the width and keep checking, but there is a better way: call the width x, write the area as x times x plus five, and set it equal to twenty-four. The equation you get is a quadratic, and solving it gives the one width that works. · A quadratic is not a formula to memorise. It is a relationship in which one quantity depends on the square of another, so its graph is a curve rather than a straight line. The curve can cross the x-axis twice, once, or not at all, and those crossings are the solutions. The factorised form, the completed square and the discriminant are three ways of reading the same curve. This lesson teaches what each one tells you, so a method you have not seen is still a problem you can start. · The explanation · A quadratic describes a curve, and its roots are where the curve meets the axis · A quadratic expression has an x squared term as its highest power, such as x squared plus five x plus six. Its graph is a parabola: a smooth U-shape that opens upwards when the x squared coefficient is positive and downwards when it is negative. The solutions of the equation are the x-values where the curve crosses the x-axis, because those are the points where the expression equals zero. A curve can cross twice, just touch the axis once, or miss it entirely, so a quadratic can have two, one or no real solutions. · That geometric picture is the check on every algebraic answer. If factorising gives two roots, the parabola should cross the axis at those two values. If the discriminant says there are no real roots, the curve should sit entirely above or entirely below the axis. An answer that disagrees with the picture is not a small slip; one of the two representations is wrong, and the disagreement is the information you need. · Factorising works because a product can be zero only when a factor is zero · The zero product property is the engine of this method: if two numbers multiply to zero, at least one of them must be zero. So if x plus two times x plus three equals zero, then either x plus two is zero or x plus three is zero. That gives x equals negative two or x equals negative three. The step is not a trick for moving numbers across the equals sign; it is a fact about multiplication that turns one quadratic equation into two linear equations. · Factorising reverses expansion. Expanding x plus two times x plus three gives x squared plus five x plus six, so a quadratic whose constant and middle coefficient come from the same pair can be written back as a product. The pair must multiply to the constant term and add to the x coefficient. When the x squared coefficient is not one, the pair has to account for that coefficient as well, which is why checking by expanding is not optional: it is how you know the factors are right before you rely on them. · Completing the square and the discriminant answer different questions · Completing the square rewrites the quadratic around its turning point. Half the x coefficient, square it, and add and subtract it so the value is unchanged: x squared plus six x plus five becomes x plus three squared minus four. The bracket shows that the smallest value is negative four, reached at x equals negative three, which is the vertex. That form is useful when the question asks for a maximum, a minimum or a turning point rather than a crossing. · The discriminant, b squared minus four a c, answers how many real roots exist before you find them. A positive value gives two roots, zero gives one repeated root, and a negative value gives no real roots. It is a check on the graph and on the factorisation, not a substitute for them. A learner who knows all three forms can choose the one that fits the question instead of applying the only procedure they remember. · Diagrams and representations · The same quadratic in expanded and factorised form. The factors are the two numbers that multiply to six and add to five. · x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) · Expanding the right-hand side returns the left-hand side exactly. The roots are the values that make a bracket zero, so they are negative two and negative three, not positive two and positive three. · A rectangle split into four regions. The x-by-x square has area x squared; the two x-by-number strips contribute five x; the corner contributes six. · (x + 2)(x + 3) = x² + 2x + 3x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6 · The area model shows why expanding works: every term in one bracket meets every term in the other, and the two x-strips combine into the middle term. · The discriminant is the part under the square root in the quadratic formula. Its sign decides how many times the parabola meets the x-axis. · x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a   ·   Δ = b² − 4ac · A positive discriminant gives two real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and a negative discriminant gives no real roots. The formula still works, but the square root of a negative number is not real. · Worked examples · Solve x² + 5x + 6 = 0 by factorising. · Look for two numbers that multiply to six and add to five: two and three. · Why: The constant term is the product of the two numbers in the brackets, and the x coefficient is their sum. Checking both conditions before writing the brackets prevents a pair that fits one but not the other. · Write the quadratic as (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0. · Why: Expanding gives back x squared plus five x plus six, so the factorised form is equivalent. The equation has not changed; only the way it is written has. · Use the zero product property: x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0, so x = −2 or x = −3. · Why: A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero. Each bracket therefore gives a linear equation, and solving both gives both roots. The signs are negative because each bracket is set to zero, not to the number inside it. · Answer: x = −2 or x = −3 · A rectangle is five centimetres longer than it is wide and has an area of 24 square centimetres. Find its width. · Let the width be x, so the length is x + 5, and write the area equation x(x + 5) = 24. · Why: Area is width times length. Naming the width first means the length can be written from the same variable, so the equation has one unknown rather than two. · Expand and rearrange: x² + 5x − 24 = 0, then factorise as (x + 8)(x − 3) = 0. · Why: The equation must equal zero before the zero product property can be used. The pair eight and negative three multiplies to negative twenty-four and adds to five, which matches the expanded form. · Solve the factors: x = −8 or x = 3. Reject −8 because a width cannot be negative, so the width is 3 cm. · Why: Both values solve the algebra, but only one describes the rectangle. Checking the answer against the situation is part of solving a modelled problem, not an optional extra. · Answer: The width is 3 cm, so the length is 8 cm. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: If (x + 2)(x + 3) = 6, then x + 2 = 6 or x + 3 = 6. · Why it fails: The zero product property works only when the product is zero. Six has many factor pairs, so a product of six does not force either bracket to equal six. The equation must be rearranged so one side is zero before the factors can be split. · Correct reasoning: Move every term to one side first, expand and simplify, then factorise the expression that equals zero. Only then set each factor to zero. · Wrong: (x + 2)(x + 3) = 6, so x = 4 or x = 3 · Right: x² + 5x + 6 = 6 becomes x² + 5x = 0, so x(x + 5) = 0 and x = 0 or x = −5 · Wrong belief: The roots of (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0 are positive two and positive three. · Why it fails: The roots are the values that make each bracket zero. The bracket x plus two is zero when x is negative two, not positive two. Reading the numbers inside the brackets as the roots reverses every sign. · Correct reasoning: Set each bracket equal to zero and solve the resulting small equation. The sign of the root is the opposite of the number in the bracket. · Wrong: the roots are 2 and 3 · Right: x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2, and x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3 · Wrong belief: A quadratic always has two solutions, so an answer with one root must be incomplete. · Why it fails: A repeated root is still one value, and a negative discriminant gives no real roots at all. The number of real solutions is a property of the curve, not a rule that every quadratic must produce two different numbers. · Correct reasoning: Use the discriminant or the graph to decide how many real roots exist before solving. If the discriminant is zero, say there is one repeated root; if it is negative, say there are no real roots. · Wrong: every quadratic has two different roots · Right: x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)² has one repeated root, x = 2 · Guided practice · Factorise and solve x² + 7x + 12 = 0. · Hint: Find two numbers that multiply to twelve and add to seven. Write the brackets first, then set each bracket to zero. · Solve x² − 4x = 0. · Hint: There is a common factor of x in both terms. Take it out before looking for two brackets. · A ball's height in metres after t seconds is h = 12t − 5t². When does it return to the ground? · Hint: The ground is h = 0. Factorise the right-hand side by taking out t, then solve both factors. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 16 marks. · Explain why (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0 allows you to conclude that x = −2 or x = −3, but (x + 2)(x + 3) = 6 does not allow you to conclude that x = 4 or x = 3. · 4 marks · Solve x² − 7x + 10 = 0. · 4 marks · How many real roots does x² − 4x + 5 = 0 have? Use the discriminant. · 4 marks · The graph of y = x² − 5x + 6 is a parabola. State its two x-intercepts, use the discriminant to confirm that it has two real roots, and give the equation of its axis of symmetry. · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · A rectangular stage is three metres longer than it is wide. A safety rule says its area must be at least forty square metres. Find the smallest whole-number width that satisfies the rule, and explain why the negative root is rejected. · The setting is a design constraint rather than a textbook equation, and the inequality changes what counts as an acceptable answer. The learner still has to form the quadratic, solve it and interpret the roots in context. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Factorise and solve x² + 8x + 15 = 0. (next day) · What does a negative discriminant tell you about the graph of a quadratic? (week later) · A rectangle has width x and length x + 4. Its area is 21. Form and solve the equation, and explain why one root is rejected. (month later) · Summary · A quadratic's roots are where its parabola meets the x-axis; it can have two, one or no real roots. · Factorising turns a product equal to zero into two linear equations, because a product is zero only when a factor is zero. · Completing the square reveals the turning point; the discriminant tells you how many real roots exist. · In a modelled problem, solve the algebra and then reject any root the situation cannot allow. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Algebraic expressions · maths · GCSE Mathematics, algebra: notation, collecting like terms and expanding brackets · Key Stage 3 to GCSE Foundation · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Read a term such as 5x as a coefficient multiplying an unknown, and explain the difference between 5x, 5 + x and x multiplied by x. · You will show this by: For x = 4, the learner evaluates 5x as 20, distinguishes it from 5 + x = 9, and explains that x multiplied by x is x squared rather than 2x. · Simplify an expression by collecting terms with the same letter part, and say why unlike terms cannot be merged. · You will show this by: The learner simplifies 7x + 4 − 3x + 9 to 4x + 13, groups the x terms separately from the constants, and rejects 3x + 2y = 5xy with a substitution. · Expand a single bracket by multiplying every term inside it, and evaluate the result for a given value as a check. · You will show this by: The learner expands 3(x + 4) to 3x + 12, explains why 3x + 4 is too small, and checks both forms at x = 2 by obtaining 18 from each. · Before you start · Work out 3 + 4 × 2. · Work out (3 + 4) × 2. · Why this matters · A school stores its whiteboard pens in identical boxes. Each box holds the same unknown number of pens, and there are three boxes plus four loose pens on the shelf. Writing the total as 3x + 4 is shorter than drawing every box, but it is only useful if you can still answer questions: how many pens are there if a box holds six? What happens if another teacher adds two more boxes? The expression is a compact description of a quantity, not a code to memorise. · Algebra begins when a number is not known yet but still has to be counted, combined and compared. A letter is a name for that number, and the number in front of it says how many copies are being counted. The same letter can stand for different values in different problems, but within one expression it stands for one value. This lesson teaches three moves that follow from that idea: collecting terms that describe the same kind of thing, expanding a bracket that multiplies a whole quantity, and substituting a value to check that the expression still means what it did before. · The explanation · A letter is a number with a name, not a label to ignore · In the expression 5x, the 5 is called the coefficient and the x is the unknown. The expression means five copies of x added together, so if x is 4 the value is 20. It does not mean five followed by four, and it does not mean five plus four. The coefficient tells you how many of the unknown quantity you have; the letter tells you which quantity is being counted. That is why 5x and 5 + x are different expressions even though both contain the same two symbols. · A letter can stand for a variable, a number that changes between cases, or for an unknown, a number we have not found yet. In a formula for the cost of n notebooks at £3 each, n is a variable because the number of notebooks can change. In the question 'three boxes and four loose pens make twenty-two pens', x is an unknown because there is one value to find. The algebra is the same in both cases: substitute a value and the expression becomes a number. Keeping that meaning in view prevents the common mistake of treating x as a physical object or as a shorthand for the digit 1. · Only like terms can be counted together · Terms are the parts of an expression separated by addition or subtraction. In 7x + 4 − 3x + 9 there are four terms: two x terms and two constants. The x terms are like terms because their letter part is exactly the same; the constants are also like terms, because they have no letter part at all. Collecting 7x and −3x gives 4x, and collecting 4 and 9 gives 13, so the expression simplifies to 4x + 13. The order of the terms does not change the value, but grouping the families makes the count visible. · Terms with different letter parts cannot be merged by adding their coefficients. In 3x + 2y, x and y are different unknowns, so the expression describes three of one thing and two of another; it stays as 3x + 2y. Writing 5xy invents a product that was never in the question, and the error is easy to expose by substitution: with x = y = 2 the original expression is 10, while 5xy is 20. The same rule separates x and x squared. One x is a length, x squared is an area, and 3x + 2x squared cannot become 5x squared or 5x cubed because the letter parts name different-sized quantities. · Expanding multiplies a whole bracket, not only its first term · A bracket groups terms into one quantity. In 3(x + 4), the whole amount x + 4 is being tripled, so both the x and the 4 must be tripled: 3x + 12. The area model makes the reason visible. Draw a rectangle three units high, split its width into a part labelled x and a part labelled 4. The large cell has area 3x, the narrow cell has area 12, and the total area is the sum of the two cells. Expanding is simply writing the two cell areas separately instead of naming the whole rectangle at once. · The same rule applies when a bracket contains subtraction or when the factor is negative. In 4(2x − 3), the 4 multiplies both 2x and −3, giving 8x − 12. In −2(x + 5), the negative sign belongs to the factor, so both products change sign: −2x − 10. A useful check is to substitute a number after expanding. At x = 1, 4(2x − 3) is 4 × (−1) = −4, and 8x − 12 is 8 − 12 = −4; if the two values disagree, a term was missed or a sign was lost. · Substitution is the check that the expression still means the same thing · Substitution means replacing every copy of the letter with a number and evaluating the result. It is the most direct test of a simplification because the original and the simplified expression must give the same value for every allowed number. Take 7x + 4 − 3x + 9 and its simplification 4x + 13. At x = 2 the original is 14 + 4 − 6 + 9 = 21, and the simplified expression is 8 + 13 = 21. If a learner had written 4x + 9, the value would be 17, and the check would locate the missing constant immediately. · Substitution also turns an expression into a tool for a situation. If a rectangle's width is x centimetres and its length is twice the width plus five centimetres, the perimeter is 2x + 2(2x + 5), which simplifies to 6x + 10. At x = 8 the perimeter is 58 centimetres. The algebra has not changed the rectangle; it has made the relationship short enough to evaluate, compare and use in a second problem. The final substitution is not an optional extra: it is how the expression is connected back to the quantity it describes. · Diagrams and representations · A coefficient counts copies of one unknown. Three boxes and four loose counters are three copies of x plus four, not the digits three and four placed side by side. · 3x + 4 · The 3 tells you there are three boxes; the x names what is in a box. The 4 counts loose counters, so it is a separate family and cannot be merged with the boxes. · A rectangle three units high with widths x and 4 splits into two cells. The cell areas are 3x and 12, so the whole area is their sum. · 3(x + 4) = 3 × x + 3 × 4 = 3x + 12 · The area model explains why every term inside the bracket is multiplied. The 12 is not an optional extra; it is the area of the second cell. · Collecting like terms is grouping by the letter part first. The x terms and the constants are counted in separate families, then written together. · 7x + 4 − 3x + 9 = (7x − 3x) + (4 + 9) = 4x + 13 · The x terms combine to four copies of x, while the constants combine to thirteen. The two results stay separate because they describe different kinds of quantity. · Worked examples · Simplify 7x + 4 − 3x + 9. · Group the x terms together and the constants together: 7x − 3x and 4 + 9. · Why: Only terms with the same letter part can be counted together. Separating the families before calculating makes it harder to merge an x term with a constant by mistake. · Subtract the x coefficients: 7 − 3 = 4, so the x terms make 4x. · Why: The coefficients count copies of the same unknown, so their counts subtract while the letter part stays x. · Add the constants: 4 + 9 = 13, and write the simplified expression as 4x + 13. · Why: The constants are a separate family, so thirteen remains a constant. The answer contains both the 4 from the x terms and the 13 from the constants. · Answer: 4x + 13 · Expand and simplify 3(2x − 5) + 4x. · Multiply both terms inside the bracket by 3: 3 × 2x = 6x and 3 × (−5) = −15. · Why: The bracket is one quantity being tripled, so every term inside it is tripled; multiplying only the 2x would leave the −5 at its original size. · Write the expansion as 6x − 15 + 4x, then collect the x terms. · Why: The 6x and the 4x are like terms, while the −15 is a constant. Collecting the like terms gives 6x + 4x = 10x. · The simplified expression is 10x − 15; check it at x = 2: the original gives 3(−1) + 8 = 5, and the answer gives 20 − 15 = 5. · Why: The substitution produces the same value from both forms, which confirms that the expansion and the collection preserved the expression. The answer contains the 10 from the x terms and the 15 from the constant. · Answer: 10x − 15 · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: 3x + 2y simplifies to 5xy because the coefficients add and the letters join together. · Why it fails: Adding counts how many copies of each kind you have. The x and y are different kinds, so their counts cannot be merged, and joining the letters turns a sum into a product that was never there. At x = y = 2 the original expression is 10, while 5xy is 20. · Correct reasoning: Keep terms with different letter parts separate. Write 3x + 2y as it stands, and substitute a value into both the original and any proposed simplification to show that the values differ. · Wrong: 3x + 2y = 5xy · Right: 3x + 2y stays 3x + 2y, because x and y are unlike terms · Wrong belief: 3(x + 4) expands to 3x + 4 because the 3 multiplies the x but leaves the 4 alone. · Why it fails: The bracket groups x + 4 as one quantity, and the 3 multiplies that whole quantity. The 4 is a part of the grouped amount, so it must be multiplied too. At x = 2 the true value is 18, while 3x + 4 is 10. · Correct reasoning: Draw the two cells of the area model or write the multiplication over both terms: 3 × x plus 3 × 4. Then substitute a value into the bracket and into the expansion; a mismatch means a term was missed. · Wrong: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4 · Right: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12 · Wrong belief: x multiplied by x is 2x, because the two x terms add their coefficients. · Why it fails: Multiplication and addition are different operations. Two copies of x added together make 2x; two copies multiplied together make x squared, because the letter is used as a factor twice. At x = 3, 2x is 6 while x squared is 9. · Correct reasoning: Ask whether the expression is counting copies or multiplying factors. Use the area model for a product: a square of side x has area x squared, not twice x. Keep the coefficient and the power separate in your written working. · Wrong: x × x = 2x · Right: x × x = x squared, while x + x = 2x · Guided practice · Simplify 5x + 8 − 2x + 3. · Hint: Separate the x terms from the constants before doing any arithmetic. Only terms in the same family can be combined. · Expand 2(3x + 4). · Hint: The 2 multiplies the whole bracket, so it must reach both the 3x and the 4. · Evaluate 4x − 3 when x = −2. · Hint: Put the negative value in brackets before multiplying, so the sign travels with the number. Multiplication is completed before the subtraction. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 12 marks. · Explain why 3x + 2y cannot be simplified to 5xy, and why 3(x + 4) expands to 3x + 12 rather than 3x + 4. Use a substitution in at least one of your explanations. · 4 marks · Simplify 8x + 5 − 3x + 2. · 4 marks · Expand 4(2x − 3). · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · A rectangle has width x centimetres and length 2x + 5 centimetres. Write and simplify an expression for its perimeter, then work out the perimeter when x = 8. · The lesson simplifies expressions and expands a single bracket in a worked example. Here the learner must choose the perimeter structure, form two copies of each dimension, expand the bracket, collect the resulting terms and then evaluate the simplified expression in the original situation. The algebra is familiar; the quantity and the order of the steps are not given. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Simplify 4x + 3x − 2. (next day) · Expand 5(x − 2). (week later) · Why is 3x + 2x squared not equal to 5x squared? (month later) · Summary · A coefficient counts copies of an unknown: 3x means three copies of x, not three plus x. · Only terms with exactly the same letter part can be collected; 3x + 2y and 3x + 2x squared stay separate. · Expanding multiplies every term inside the bracket, so 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. · Substitute a value into the original and the simplified form; the values must agree. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Data representation · maths · GCSE Mathematics, statistics: bar charts, line graphs, pie charts and scatter graphs; choosing, constructing and criticising a representation · Key Stage 3 to GCSE Foundation · version 1.1.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Choose a chart from the type of data and the question being asked, and explain why the alternatives are weaker. · You will show this by: For unordered categories the learner chooses a bar chart, for change over time a line graph, for shares of one whole a pie chart, and for two measured variables a scatter graph, giving a reason for each choice rather than naming a favourite. · Read a chart honestly by finding its total, its scale and its baseline, and explain how a truncated axis changes the comparison the picture makes. · You will show this by: Given bars of 32 and 36 on axes starting at 0 and at 30, the learner says the true rise is 4 (12.5%) while the truncated chart draws heights of 2 and 6, and that the labels are true even when the visual ratio is not. · Construct a bar chart and a pie chart from a frequency table, calculate each pie angle, and state what the chart does not show. · You will show this by: For 60 learners travelling by walk, bus, car and cycle the learner obtains 90°, 144°, 72° and 54°, checks the angles sum to 360°, and explains that the pie shows each share but not the total of 60 or the count in each category. · Before you start · Find the mean of 4, 6, 8 and 10. · The mean of five values is 12. What is their total? · Why this matters · A local paper reports that cycling to a school has 'tripled'. The chart shows two bars, 32 last year and 36 this year, on an axis that starts at 30 rather than 0. The bars are 2 and 6 units tall, so the second really does look three times the first. The numbers rose by 4, which is 12.5%. Every label on the chart is true, and the picture still tells a story the data do not support. · A chart is not a photograph of a data set; it is an argument about which comparison matters. The type of chart decides what is easy to see: bars compare categories, a line shows change through an ordered sequence, a pie shows each category's share of one whole, and a scatter shows whether two measured variables move together. The scale decides how large a difference looks, and the total decides what a share means. Reading a chart critically means asking three questions before believing it — what is the total, what does the axis do, and what is missing — and those questions are also the checklist for making an honest one. · The explanation · The question decides the chart · A bar chart compares counts or amounts across categories. Its bars are separate because the categories are separate: football, netball and swimming have no order, so the gap between the bars is information. A line graph is different. It is used when the horizontal axis is an ordered sequence, usually time, because the segment between two points asserts that the values in between are meaningful. Drawing a line through favourite colours joins points that have no in-between, so the trend it appears to show was invented by the chart. · A pie chart is for parts of one whole: every category is a share of the same total, and the angles sum to 360°. A scatter graph is for two measured variables on the same individual, such as height and shoe size, and it can show a relationship without either variable being a category. Choosing a chart is therefore part of answering the question. A pie with twelve thin slices is unreadable; a bar chart with forty categories is a wall; a line through unordered categories is a false claim about continuity. The chart should make the intended comparison easy, not decorate the table. · A scale is part of the argument · In a bar chart the length of the bar encodes the value, so the baseline is part of the measurement. If the axis starts at 0, a value of 36 is 90% of a full-scale 40 and a value of 32 is 80%, which is the ratio the numbers actually have. If the axis starts at 30, the same two values become bars of 6 and 2, and the second looks three times the first. The labels are still correct; the lengths are not proportional to the values, so the visual comparison is false. A truncated bar chart is not lying about the numbers, it is lying with the lengths. · A line graph encodes value by position rather than length, so a truncated vertical axis exaggerates a change without changing the shape of the line. That can be legitimate when the interesting variation is small, provided the axis is labelled and the reader is told, but it is misleading when the picture is presented as the whole story. Equal intervals matter on both axes: a gap of 10 must be the same distance wherever it appears, or the slope and the spacing stop meaning anything. Axes need names and units, because a number without a unit cannot be checked. · Pie charts encode shares, not counts · A pie chart turns each category's share of the total into an angle. The whole circle is 360°, so a category with a quarter of the total gets a quarter of 360°, which is 90°. For 60 learners travelling by walk, bus, car and cycle in the counts 15, 24, 12 and 9, the shares are 25%, 40%, 20% and 15%, and the angles are 90°, 144°, 72° and 54°. The four angles must add to 360°; if they do not, either a count or a division is wrong. The largest sector is the bus at 144°, which is 40% of the learners. · The angle is a share, so it cannot tell you a count without the total. Half of 40 learners is 20, while a quarter of 200 is 50: the second slice is smaller and the number of learners is larger. Across two pie charts with different totals, a bigger angle does not mean more items; within one chart, it does mean a larger share. A pie also hides the total itself, because the circle is always 100% however many people were asked. That is why a report should print the total and the counts beside the chart rather than leaving the reader to infer them. · Reading critically: total, scale, missing · Three questions catch most misleading charts. What is the total? A percentage without a base is unreadable, and two charts with different totals cannot be compared by angle. What does each axis do? Check where the vertical axis starts, whether the intervals are equal, and whether both axes are labelled with units. What is missing? Non-responses, merged categories, a change in what was counted, or a source that stopped at a convenient year can matter more than anything drawn. A chart can be accurate in every number and still mislead by what it leaves out. · The defence is arithmetic rather than suspicion. Read the values, recompute a share or a difference, and compare it with what the picture appears to claim. In a scatter graph, a pattern is not a cause: two variables can rise together because a third factor drives both, and the genome's next concept, correlation, is where that distinction is taught. When you make a chart, state the total, the scale and the units, and start bars at zero, so a reader can check the argument instead of trusting the shape. · Diagrams and representations · A frequency table becomes a bar chart by using each count as the height of its bar. The bars start at zero so their lengths stay proportional to the counts. · football 12 · netball 8 · swimming 5 · athletics 3 · total 28 · scale 0 to 12, step 2 · The tallest bar is football at 12 and the shortest is athletics at 3, a ratio of four to one that the zero baseline preserves. If the axis started at 10, those same bars would be 2 and -7 units, which is impossible, or 2 and 0, which reverses the order. · A pie chart turns each category's share into an angle. The whole circle is the total, so every angle is share × 360° and the angles must add to 360°. · travel to school, 60 learners: walk 15, bus 24, car 12, cycle 9   ·   angles 90°, 144°, 72°, 54°   ·   sum 360°   ·   bus = 40% · The bus sector is the largest at 144°, which is 40% of the 60 learners, or 24 people. The pie shows the share clearly and the total not at all: the same angles would describe 6 learners or 600. · The same two values can look almost equal or three times apart depending on where the bar axis starts. The numbers do not change; the lengths do. · cycling 32 → 36   ·   true change +4 = 12.5%   ·   axis 0–40: heights 80% and 90%   ·   axis 30–40: heights 2 and 6 = 3× · On a zero baseline the rise is one tenth of a full bar and looks small, which is honest. Starting at 30 draws the same rise as a bar three times as tall, which is the picture the headline 'tripled' came from. · Worked examples · A table records favourite sports: football 12, netball 8, swimming 5 and athletics 3. Build a bar chart and state its scale and total. · Add the counts to find the total: 12 + 8 + 5 + 3 = 28 learners were asked. · Why: The total is the whole the bars are parts of. Without it, a reader cannot turn a count into a share or check that every learner is represented once. · Choose a bar chart, because the categories have no natural order and the question compares their counts. · Why: A line would imply that football, netball and swimming sit on an ordered scale, which they do not. A pie would show shares, but the comparison asked for is between counts. · Set the vertical axis from 0 to 12 with steps of 2, label it 'number of learners', and draw each bar to its count. · Why: A zero baseline keeps bar length proportional to the count. A step of 2 fits the largest value of 12 without compressing the smaller bars into illegibility. · Check the chart against the table: the football bar is 12, the athletics bar is 3, and the four bars account for all 28 learners. · Why: The chart has to preserve both the individual values and the total. A bar drawn to the wrong height is a false number even when the table beside it is right. · Answer: A bar chart with a 0–12 axis, bars of 12, 8, 5 and 3, labelled in learners; total 28. · A survey of 60 learners records how they travel: walk 15, bus 24, car 12, cycle 9. Draw a pie chart, calculating each angle. · Check the total: 15 + 24 + 12 + 9 = 60. · Why: Every share is a fraction of this total, and a pie is only valid when the categories account for the whole group exactly once. · Turn each count into a share and then an angle: 15/60 × 360° = 90°, 24/60 × 360° = 144°, 12/60 × 360° = 72°, 9/60 × 360° = 54°. · Why: The angle is the share of the circle, so the same fraction that gives the proportion gives the angle. Multiplying by 360° converts a fraction of the whole into degrees. · Check the angles sum to 360°: 90 + 144 + 72 + 54 = 360. · Why: The four sectors must fill the circle exactly. A sum above or below 360° means a count, a total or a division is wrong, and the check catches it before the chart is drawn. · The bus sector is 144°, the largest; it is 40% of the learners, which is 24 people. The pie shows the share but not the 60 or the 24 unless they are printed beside it. · Why: A reader can see that bus is the largest share without knowing how many learners were asked. The count needs the total, which is why the total belongs in the title or the key. · Answer: Angles 90°, 144°, 72° and 54°, summing to 360°; bus is the largest share at 40% (24 learners). · A chart shows cycling rising from 32 to 36 with a vertical axis starting at 30. Explain what the picture exaggerates and what the true change is. · Find the true change: 36 - 32 = 4, and 4 ÷ 32 = 0.125, so the rise is 12.5%. · Why: The percentage compares the change with the starting value. It is the honest size of the change, independent of how the axis is drawn. · Read the bar heights the axis actually draws: with a baseline of 30, the bars are 36 - 30 = 6 and 32 - 30 = 2. · Why: Bar length encodes value above the baseline. The labels 32 and 36 are true, but the lengths a reader compares are 2 and 6. · Compare the visual ratio with the true ratio: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, while 36 ÷ 32 = 1.125. The chart makes a 12.5% rise look like a tripling. · Why: The reader compares lengths, not printed labels. A truncated axis turns a small change into a large-looking one, which is why the headline and the picture agree with each other and not with the data. · The honest chart starts at 0, where the bars are 32 and 36 and the true rise of 4 (12.5%) looks small; the 30-based chart's heights of 2 and 6 are what turn that rise into a three-times picture, so a truncated axis must be disclosed and the values read. · Why: A zero baseline preserves the ratio. Truncation can be legitimate, but only when it is disclosed, because the picture no longer carries the comparison on its own. · Answer: The true rise is 4, or 12.5%; the 30-based axis draws bars of 2 and 6, a three-times picture, so the chart exaggerates a small change. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: A pie chart shows the counts, so a bigger slice always means more items, even when comparing two different charts. · Why it fails: A pie angle is a share of that chart's total, not a count. Half of 40 learners is 20, while a quarter of 200 is 50: the second slice is smaller and represents more learners. The circle is always 100%, so the total is invisible unless it is printed. · Correct reasoning: Use angles to compare shares within one chart, and counts to compare across charts. Print the total and the category counts beside the pie, and recompute a count from the share only when the total is known. · Wrong: the bigger slice always means more learners · Right: 50% of 40 is 20, but 25% of 200 is 50: the smaller share is more learners · Wrong belief: Any data can be shown on a line graph, because joining the points shows the trend. · Why it fails: A line asserts that the horizontal axis is ordered and that values between the points are meaningful. Favourite colours, makes of car and types of pet have no in-between, so a line through them invents a sequence and a trend that the data never had. · Correct reasoning: Use a line only when the horizontal axis is an ordered sequence, usually time. For unordered categories use a bar chart, which keeps the categories separate and does not imply a value between them. · Wrong: join favourite colours with a line to show the trend · Right: favourite colours are unordered, so they belong on separate bars · Wrong belief: Starting a bar chart's axis at 30 instead of 0 is acceptable, because the bars are still labelled with the true values. · Why it fails: A bar's length is the value above the baseline, and that length is what a reader compares. Starting at 30 turns values of 32 and 36 into bars of 2 and 6, so a 12.5% rise looks like a tripling. The labels can be true while the visual comparison is false. · Correct reasoning: Start a bar chart at zero. If a truncated axis is genuinely needed for detail, label it clearly, say that it is truncated, and expect the reader to compare the printed values rather than the bar lengths. For a line graph, check the vertical range before describing the size of a change. · Wrong: the bars are labelled 32 and 36, so the chart is honest · Right: the bars are drawn 2 and 6 units tall, which is a three-times picture for a 12.5% rise · Guided practice · A table lists favourite fruits and how many learners chose each. Which chart would you use, and why is a line graph a poor choice? · Hint: Ask whether the categories have an order. Fruit names do not sit on a scale, and a line asserts that the values between two points mean something. · A pie chart is drawn for 40 learners: 10 walk, 20 take the bus and 10 come by car. Calculate each angle and check the total. · Hint: Each angle is the category's share of 40 multiplied by 360°. The three angles must add to 360°. · A bar chart starts its vertical axis at 50. Two bars are labelled 52 and 58. What is the true difference, and what does the picture exaggerate? · Hint: Subtract the baseline from each value to find the drawn heights, then compare the ratio of the heights with the ratio of the values. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 16 marks. · A survey of 200 learners records how they travel: bus 80, walk 50, car 40, cycle 30. Calculate the pie angles, explain what the pie does not show, and explain why a bar chart of the same data should start at zero. · 4 marks · A pie chart shows that 25% of learners walk. The total is 80 learners. How many walk? · 4 marks · A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 100. Two bars are labelled 108 and 116. What is the true difference between the values? · 4 marks · A survey of 40 learners records how they travel: 10 walk, 20 take the bus and 10 come by car. Complete the table of pie-chart angles. · 4 marks · (a) Complete the angle for each category. Each cell is worth one mark. [3] · 	Walk	Bus	Car · Learners	10	20	10 · Angle (°)			 · (b) Add your three angles. What must the total be? [1] · Use it in a new situation · Two schools report their cycling. School A has 400 pupils and 40 cycle; School B has 250 pupils and 30 cycle. A headline says 'More cyclists at School B'. A second says 'Cycling is more common at School B'. Calculate the counts and the shares, and say which chart would support each headline. Then explain which claim is true, and what would reverse the second claim. · The lesson reads one chart and computes one set of pie angles. Here the learner must compare two data sets with different totals, keep the count and the share apart, decide which representation supports which sentence, and then work out what would change the answer. The arithmetic is familiar; the separation of count from share, and the fact that a total can reverse a claim, are new. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Which chart would you use for the temperature on each day of a week, and why? (next day) · A pie chart has a sector of 90°. What share of the whole is it, and what fraction? (week later) · Why should the vertical axis of a bar chart start at zero? (month later) · Summary · The question chooses the chart: bars for unordered categories, a line for an ordered sequence, a pie for parts of one whole, a scatter for two measured variables. · A bar's length encodes its value, so bars start at zero; truncating the axis can make a 12.5% rise look like a tripling even when every label is true. · A pie angle is share × 360°, the angles must sum to 360°, and the chart shows shares rather than counts or the total. · Read a chart by asking what the total is, what each axis does, and what is missing before believing the shape. · Two charts with different totals cannot be compared by angle: recompute the counts, because a smaller share of a larger total can be more items. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Motion · physics · GCSE Physics, forces and motion: distance–time and velocity–time graphs, gradient and area · Key Stage 3 to GCSE · version 1.2.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Read the gradient of a distance–time graph as speed, and distinguish instantaneous speed from average speed over a whole journey. · You will show this by: For a journey that covers 8 m in the first 4 s and then rests for 3 s, the learner reads 2 m/s from the first gradient and 0 m/s from the flat section, then calculates the average speed over the whole journey from total distance divided by total time. · Read the gradient of a velocity–time graph as acceleration and the area under it as displacement, including negative values. · You will show this by: For a cyclist who reaches 8 m/s from rest in 4 s, the learner calculates an acceleration of 2 m/s² and a distance of 16 m from the triangular area, with the units stated. · Explain why a high flat line on a distance–time graph is not a fast object, and why a flat velocity–time line is not an object at rest. · You will show this by: The learner says the height of a distance–time graph is how far away the object is, so a high flat line means it is far away and stationary; a flat velocity–time line means the velocity is constant, so the object is still moving and its displacement continues to grow. · Before you start · A straight line passes through the points (0, 0) and (4, 8). What is its gradient, and how did you find it? · A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is the average speed, and what does the answer mean? · Why this matters · A bus leaves a stop, waits at a red light, then travels steadily along a straight road. Its distance–time graph climbs, goes flat, then climbs again. The same journey drawn as velocity against time looks completely different: the bus speeds up, travels at a steady velocity, then slows to a stop. · A graph is a compact story about motion, but only if you know which question each axis answers. The gradient of a distance–time graph tells you how quickly position changes; the gradient of a velocity–time graph tells you how quickly velocity changes; the area under a velocity–time graph tells you how far the object has moved. Keeping those three readings separate is the whole of this topic, and it stops a learner from memorising formulas they cannot apply to an unfamiliar graph. · The explanation · The axes are the first sentence of the graph · Before reading any number, name the quantity on each axis and its unit. A distance–time graph plots position against time, so its vertical axis is in metres and its horizontal axis is in seconds. A velocity–time graph plots velocity against time, so its vertical axis is in metres per second. The same rising line therefore means different things on the two graphs: on the first it is a fast object, and on the second it is an object whose velocity is increasing. · The shape of the line is read between two points, not at a single point. A straight line means the gradient is constant, so the quantity represented by that gradient stays the same. A curved line means the gradient changes, so speed or acceleration is changing. A flat line means the vertical quantity is not changing, which is not the same as the object being absent or the graph being empty. · Distance–time: the gradient is speed · On a distance–time graph, gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time. Those are the units of speed, metres per second, so the gradient is the speed. A steep line means a large distance is covered in a short time, so the object is fast. A shallow line means the object is slow, and a flat line means its distance is not changing at all, so it is stationary. · For a journey with several stages, calculate the gradient of each straight section separately rather than joining the ends. A graph that rises, flattens and rises again has three different speeds, and the gradient of the whole line from start to finish is only the average velocity, not what happened at any particular moment. The average speed is a separate calculation: total distance travelled divided by total time taken. A return journey is the case that makes the difference unavoidable, because the distance travelled keeps increasing while the displacement can return to zero. · Velocity–time: the gradient is acceleration, the area is displacement · On a velocity–time graph, gradient is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, which is acceleration. A positive gradient means velocity is increasing in the positive direction; a negative gradient means it is decreasing, or becoming more negative. A flat line means the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the object is not at rest unless the flat line sits on the horizontal axis. · The area between the line and the time axis gives the displacement. Split the area into rectangles and triangles rather than looking for a single formula. A rectangle of height 8 m/s and width 6 s contributes 48 m; a triangle of height 8 m/s and base 4 s contributes 16 m. If the line crosses below the time axis, that area is negative displacement, so the object is moving back towards its starting point and the signed areas must be added rather than all counted as distance. · Signs, averages and the assumptions a graph makes · Speed is a scalar: it has size but no direction, so it is never negative. Velocity is a vector: its sign says which way the object moves. That is why a graph can show a negative velocity, and why average speed and average velocity can disagree. A runner who goes 100 m out and 100 m back in 50 s has an average speed of 4 m/s but an average velocity of zero, because the displacement is zero even though the distance travelled is 200 m. · The straight-line model assumes constant acceleration between the marked points, and it treats the motion as one-dimensional. Those assumptions are idealisations: a real car changes acceleration continuously, and a real road bends. The graph is still useful because it captures the part of the motion we care about, but an answer should say when the model is being used outside the range where it is a good approximation. · Diagrams and representations · The gradient of a straight line is the change in the vertical quantity divided by the change in the horizontal quantity. On a motion graph, the axes decide which physical quantity that gradient represents. · gradient = change in vertical value / change in horizontal value · On a distance–time graph the gradient is speed in metres per second. On a velocity–time graph the gradient is acceleration in metres per second squared. The units are the clue: dividing metres by seconds gives metres per second. · The area under a velocity–time graph is the displacement. A rectangle contributes height times width, and a triangle contributes one half times base times height. · displacement = area under velocity–time graph · A velocity of 8 m/s held for 6 s gives an area of 48 m. A velocity rising steadily from zero to 8 m/s over 4 s gives a triangle of area 16 m. The area's unit is metres because metres per second multiplied by seconds is metres. · Every reading from a motion graph carries a unit, and the unit is how you check that you have read the right feature. A bare number cannot tell you whether it is a distance, a speed or an acceleration. · distance: m · time: s · speed: m/s · velocity: m/s · acceleration: m/s² · Metres divided by seconds gives metres per second. A change in metres per second divided by seconds gives metres per second squared. If the unit does not match the question, the gradient or area has been read from the wrong graph. · The two graphs answer different questions. A distance–time graph says where the object is; a velocity–time graph says how its velocity is changing and how far it has travelled. · distance–time: height = position, gradient = speed, flat = stationary · velocity–time: height = velocity, gradient = acceleration, flat = constant velocity, area = displacement · A flat distance–time line means the object has stopped. A flat velocity–time line means the object is moving at a steady velocity. The same shape has opposite meanings because the vertical axes are different quantities. · Worked examples · A walker moves 8 m away from a sensor in the first 4 s, rests for 3 s, then walks 6 m back towards the sensor in the next 3 s. Calculate the speed during each stage, the total distance, the displacement and the average speed for the whole 10 s. · For the first stage, gradient = change in distance / change in time = 8 m / 4 s = 2 m/s. · Why: The distance–time gradient is speed, and the first section is a straight line, so the walker's speed is constant at 2 m/s away from the sensor. · The middle stage is flat, so its gradient is 0 m / 3 s = 0 m/s, which means the walker is stationary. · Why: A flat distance–time line means the distance from the sensor is not changing, so the walker is at rest for those 3 s. · The final stage has gradient = 6 m / 3 s = 2 m/s back towards the sensor, so the velocity is negative if away is positive. · Why: The distance is falling, so the change is negative; the speed is 2 m/s but the direction is opposite to the first stage. · Total distance = 8 m + 6 m = 14 m; displacement = 8 m − 6 m = 2 m away; average speed = 14 m / 10 s = 1.4 m/s. · Why: Distance counts both directions, while displacement counts the straight-line change from start to finish. Average speed uses the total distance, not the displacement. · Answer: The speeds are 2 m/s, 0 m/s and 2 m/s; the total distance is 14 m, the displacement is 2 m away from the sensor, and the average speed is 1.4 m/s. · A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to 8 m/s in 4 s, then travels at 8 m/s for 6 s. Calculate the acceleration during the first stage and the total displacement shown by the velocity–time graph. · For the first stage, acceleration = change in velocity / change in time = 8 m/s / 4 s = 2 m/s². · Why: The velocity–time gradient is acceleration. The velocity rises by 8 m/s in 4 s, so the acceleration is 2 metres per second squared. · The first stage's area is a triangle: one half times base times height = one half times 4 s times 8 m/s = 16 m. · Why: The velocity rises steadily from zero, so the area under that section is a triangle rather than a rectangle. · The second stage's area is a rectangle: 8 m/s times 6 s = 48 m. Total displacement = 16 m + 48 m = 64 m. · Why: A constant velocity for 6 s contributes height times width, and the two areas add because both stages move in the same direction. · Answer: The acceleration is 2 m/s² and the total displacement is 64 m. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: The height of a distance–time graph tells you how fast the object is moving. · Why it fails: Height is the object's distance from the starting point, not its speed. A high flat line means the object is far away and stationary, while a line starting at zero and rising steeply means the object is close but moving quickly. The speed is the gradient, which is how steeply the line rises, not how high it has reached. · Correct reasoning: Read speed from the gradient of the distance–time line. Read position from its height. A flat line at any height means zero speed. · Wrong: the line is high, so the object must be moving fast · Right: the line is high but flat, so the object is far away and stationary · Wrong belief: A flat velocity–time graph means the object has stopped. · Why it fails: A flat velocity–time line means the velocity is not changing, so the object is moving at a constant velocity. It has stopped only if the line lies on the horizontal axis at zero. A flat line above the axis shows a steady speed, and the area beneath it continues to add displacement every second. · Correct reasoning: A flat velocity–time line means zero acceleration, not zero velocity. Check the height of the line to see whether the constant velocity is zero or non-zero. · Wrong: the velocity–time line is flat, so the car is parked · Right: the line is flat at 8 m/s, so the car is moving steadily at 8 m/s · Wrong belief: Negative acceleration always means the object is slowing down. · Why it fails: Acceleration is a vector. A negative acceleration means the acceleration points in the negative direction. An object already moving in the negative direction speeds up when its acceleration is negative, while an object moving in the positive direction slows down. The sign alone does not tell you whether the speed is rising or falling; you need the direction of motion as well. · Correct reasoning: Compare the signs of velocity and acceleration. If they point the same way, the object speeds up; if they point in opposite directions, it slows down. Negative acceleration is not a synonym for deceleration. · Wrong: acceleration is negative, so the object must be slowing · Right: the object is moving left and accelerating left, so its speed is increasing · Guided practice · A distance–time graph shows a cyclist moving 6 m in the first 2 s, stopping for 3 s, then moving 9 m in the next 3 s. Calculate the speed in each stage and the average speed over the whole 8 s. · Hint: Find the gradient of each straight section separately. For the average, add the distances first and divide by the total time, including the stop. · A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes uniformly to rest in 5 s. Calculate its acceleration and the distance it travels while braking. · Hint: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration. The distance is the area of the triangle under the line. · A velocity–time graph rises from 0 to 6 m/s in 2 s, stays at 6 m/s for 3 s, then falls to 0 m/s in 3 s. Calculate the acceleration in each stage and the total displacement. · Hint: Use the gradient for each acceleration and split the area into a triangle, a rectangle and a triangle. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 18 marks. · A velocity–time graph shows a train moving at 12 m/s for 4 s, then decelerating uniformly to rest in 6 s. Describe what the gradient and the area represent in each stage, and calculate the total displacement. Explain why the deceleration does not make the displacement negative. · 4 marks · A train accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 6.0 s. Calculate the distance it travels during this acceleration, stating the unit. · 4 marks · A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track and returns to the starting point in 80 s. Explain why the average speed is 5 m/s but the average velocity is zero. · 4 marks · A cyclist's velocity–time graph is the straight line y = 2x + 4, where y is velocity in m/s and x is time in seconds. Give the line on the grid, then read the velocity at 3 s from the line you have drawn. · 3 marks · (a) Give two points on the line y = 2x + 4. [2] · x · y · 0 · 0 · 3 · 9 · 6 · 18 · (b) Use your line to read the velocity at 3 s. [1] · Use the graph you drew in part (a) at x = 3. · Plot the cyclist's velocity from the table: at 0 s it is 4 m/s, at 2 s it is 8 m/s, at 4 s it is 12 m/s and at 6 s it is 16 m/s. Join the points with a straight line, then read the velocity at 5 s. · 3 marks · (a) Plot the four points and join them with a straight line. [2] · x · y · 0 · 0 · 3 · 9 · 6 · 18 · (b) Use your line to read the velocity at 5 s. [1] · Use the graph you drew in part (a) at x = 5. · Use it in a new situation · A ball is thrown vertically upwards and caught at the same height. Its velocity–time graph is a straight line with a negative gradient throughout. Explain what the gradient represents, why the line crosses the time axis, and why the displacement over the whole flight is zero. · The lesson used horizontal journeys and a braking cyclist. Here the same velocity–time reading is applied to vertical motion, where the sign of the velocity changes while the acceleration stays constant, so the learner must follow the direction as well as the size. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · State what the gradient of a distance–time graph represents, and what a flat section means. (next day) · A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s. Calculate its acceleration and the distance travelled. (week later) · Explain the difference between a flat line on a distance–time graph and a flat line on a velocity–time graph. (month later) · Summary · On a distance–time graph, gradient is speed and height is position; a flat line means the object is stationary. · On a velocity–time graph, gradient is acceleration and the area under the line is displacement; a flat line means constant velocity, not rest. · Average speed uses total distance over total time, while average velocity uses displacement over time; a return journey can have a non-zero average speed and zero average velocity. · A signed velocity–time graph can have negative area, which subtracts from displacement rather than adding to the distance travelled. · OpenMind-authored lesson.
