documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Photosynthesis · biology · GCSE Biology, bioenergetics: photosynthesis and limiting factors · Key Stage 3 to GCSE · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · State the reactants, products and location of photosynthesis, and explain what the plant does with each product. · You will show this by: The learner names carbon dioxide and water as reactants, glucose and oxygen as products, places the process in the chloroplast, and says glucose is used for growth, storage as starch or respiration, while oxygen leaves the leaf. · Read a rate-versus-light-intensity graph and identify which factor is limiting at a given point. · You will show this by: At the steep part of the curve the learner names light intensity as limiting; at the plateau the learner says another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, has taken over and proposes how to test that. · Explain why a plant both photosynthesises and respires, and why the net gas exchange of a leaf depends on which rate is greater. · You will show this by: The learner states that respiration runs all the time in every living cell, while photosynthesis runs only in the light, so in darkness a leaf takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and in bright light the reverse is net. · Before you start · What does an enzyme do, and what happens to it when it gets too hot? · Why does a reaction inside a cell stop rising in rate once the enzyme is saturated? · Why this matters · A potato left in a dark cupboard for a month grows a pale, spindly shoot. Put the same potato on a windowsill and the shoot is short and green. The plant had the same store of energy in both places. What it did not have in the cupboard was light. · Photosynthesis converts light energy into the chemical energy of glucose. Everything a plant builds, and every food chain on Earth, starts with that conversion. But a plant is not a solar panel that runs only in sunshine: it also respires, continuously, in every cell. Understanding the ratio between those two rates is what explains why a leaf's gas exchange changes direction between day and night. · The explanation · The reaction, and where it happens · Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide and water and uses light energy to build glucose, releasing oxygen. In symbols, six carbon dioxide plus six water give one glucose plus six oxygen. The reaction happens in chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light. A plant without chloroplasts — a root cell, for example — cannot photosynthesise, which is why roots depend on the leaves for sugar. · The glucose is not simply fuel. Some is used in respiration, some is converted to starch for storage, some becomes cellulose for cell walls, and some is combined with nitrogen to make amino acids. The oxygen is a by-product of splitting water and leaves the leaf by diffusion. · Rate is set by whichever factor is in shortest supply · Increasing light intensity increases the rate, but only until something else runs out. On a graph of rate against light, the rising section means light is limiting: more light gives more photosynthesis. The flat section means light is no longer limiting; carbon dioxide concentration or temperature has become the bottleneck, and adding more light changes nothing. · This is the same saturation idea that governs enzymes, and it is the reason a greenhouse raises carbon dioxide as well as letting light in. Temperature is a limiting factor in a different way: it speeds up the enzyme-controlled reactions, but beyond an optimum the enzymes denature and the rate falls sharply. · Plants respire too, all the time · Respiration releases energy from glucose and happens in every living cell, in darkness as well as light. Photosynthesis only happens where there is chlorophyll and light. So a leaf is running both processes at once during the day, and only respiration at night. · That is why gas exchange changes direction. In darkness, oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide diffuses out. In bright light, photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration, so carbon dioxide diffuses in and oxygen diffuses out. At the compensation point the two rates are equal and there is no net exchange, which is a fact about a ratio rather than about the plant switching processes on and off. · Testing the claim, not just stating it · A pondweed in water releases oxygen bubbles. Moving the lamp further away lowers the bubble count, and plotting rate against distance shows the falling curve. But bubbles are a proxy: they count a product of photosynthesis, and the count is only meaningful if everything else — temperature, carbon dioxide concentration, the plant's health — is held constant. · A claim about a limiting factor is a claim about a controlled comparison. Vary one factor, hold the rest, and look for the point where the rate stops responding. Without the control, a change in rate could be attributed to the wrong cause, which is the single most common weakness in answers to this kind of question. · Diagrams and representations · Light is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplast, which drives the splitting of water and the fixing of carbon dioxide into glucose; oxygen leaves the leaf by diffusion because its concentration inside the leaf is higher than outside. · 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ · The arrow is driven by light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. Remove the light and the process stops, even though every reactant is still present. · A palisade cell is packed with chloroplasts near the top of the leaf, because that position and density let it absorb the most light per unit area before the light is intercepted by cells below. · palisade mesophyll: chloroplast-dense, upper layer · The structure exists for the function. A leaf that put its chloroplasts at the bottom would absorb far less light for the same cost of building the leaf. · A leaf has stomata on its underside and air spaces between spongy mesophyll cells, so that carbon dioxide can diffuse in and oxygen out along a short, moist path. · stoma + air space: short diffusion path, large surface area · Diffusion needs a gradient and a short path. The leaf's internal architecture supplies both, which is why a thick, dry leaf would photosynthesise poorly even in full sun. · Pondweed is placed at increasing distances from a lamp and the oxygen bubbles are counted for one minute at each distance. Temperature and carbon dioxide concentration are kept constant, and the plant is left to settle before each count. · distance 10, 20, 30, 40 cm · bubbles per minute recorded · other factors controlled · Bubble count is a proxy for rate. The controlled variables are what make a fall in the count attributable to distance rather than to the plant warming up or running out of carbon dioxide. · Worked examples · A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed at increasing light intensities. The rate rises and then levels off. Explain what is happening at each part of the graph and how the student could test the explanation. · On the rising section, identify light intensity as the limiting factor, because increasing it increases the rate. · Why: A factor is limiting when changing it changes the rate. The rise is direct evidence that light is the factor in shortest supply at those points. · At the plateau, conclude that light is no longer limiting and that another factor has taken over — most likely carbon dioxide concentration or temperature. · Why: The rate has stopped responding to the variable being changed. That only happens when a different factor has become the bottleneck, so the plateau is evidence about a second factor rather than about light. · Propose a controlled test: repeat the experiment with a higher carbon dioxide concentration, keeping light intensity, temperature and the plant the same, and see whether the plateau is higher. · Why: The claim is that carbon dioxide is now limiting. Testing it means changing only that factor; if the plateau rises, the claim is supported, and if it does not, temperature is the better candidate. · Answer: Light is limiting on the rising section and carbon dioxide (or temperature) is limiting at the plateau; raising carbon dioxide while holding everything else constant should raise the plateau if that is the limiting factor. · A leaf is sealed in a transparent chamber. In bright light the carbon dioxide concentration in the chamber falls; in darkness it rises. Explain both observations using the two processes happening in the leaf. · Identify that photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and respiration releases it, and that both are happening in the leaf. · Why: The observation cannot be explained by one process alone. Both are always available; what differs between light and dark is the rate of photosynthesis. · In bright light, conclude that the rate of photosynthesis exceeds the rate of respiration, so the net effect is uptake of carbon dioxide. · Why: Net exchange is a difference between two rates, not a switch. Photosynthesis is using carbon dioxide faster than respiration is producing it. · In darkness, conclude that photosynthesis has stopped while respiration continues, so the net effect is release of carbon dioxide. · Why: Respiration does not depend on light. With photosynthesis at zero, the only process moving carbon dioxide is respiration, which releases it. · Answer: In light, photosynthesis outpaces respiration and the leaf takes up carbon dioxide; in darkness photosynthesis stops while respiration continues, so the leaf releases carbon dioxide. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: Plants photosynthesise instead of respiring, so they only take in carbon dioxide. · Why it fails: Respiration happens in every living cell, continuously, including in plants and including in the light. Photosynthesis is an additional process, not a replacement. If a plant did not respire, it could not release the energy stored in the glucose it has just made. · Correct reasoning: Both processes run during the day; only respiration runs at night. What you observe as gas exchange is the NET of the two rates, which is why the direction can reverse. · Wrong: plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, full stop · Right: plants respire always and photosynthesise in light; net gas exchange depends on which rate is greater · Wrong belief: The flat part of a light-intensity graph means photosynthesis has stopped. · Why it fails: A plateau is a rate that has stopped rising, not a rate that has fallen to zero. Photosynthesis is still happening at the plateau — often faster than at any earlier point on the graph. What has stopped is the response to light. · Correct reasoning: Read the plateau as a change of limiting factor. The rate is set by something else now, and the graph tells you that increasing light further will not help. · Wrong: the rate is zero, so photosynthesis has stopped · Right: the rate is constant and high, so another factor has become limiting · Wrong belief: A plant gets its food from the soil. · Why it fails: Soil supplies water and mineral ions, not energy. The mass of a tree comes overwhelmingly from carbon dioxide in the air, fixed into glucose by photosynthesis. A plant in distilled water with light and air can still grow; a plant with soil and no light cannot. · Correct reasoning: Separate raw materials from energy. Water and minerals are raw materials absorbed by roots; the energy and the carbon come from light and air. Glucose is the plant's food, and the plant makes it. · Wrong: the plant eats nutrients from the soil · Right: the plant builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light, and takes minerals from the soil · Guided practice · A greenhouse is kept warm and well lit, but the plants still grow slowly. Suggest one change that could increase the rate of photosynthesis, and explain your reasoning. · Hint: Warm and well lit means two factors are already supplied. Which reactant has not been mentioned? · Explain why a variegated leaf with white edges photosynthesises less than an all-green leaf of the same size. · Hint: What does the white part lack, and what is that substance for? · A leaf in bright light is found to have a higher oxygen concentration inside than outside. Explain why oxygen leaves the leaf. · Hint: Diffusion moves particles from where there are more to where there are fewer. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 20 marks. · Explain why the net gas exchange of a leaf changes direction between day and night. · 4 marks · A student claims that a plant placed in a sealed lit container will eventually stop photosynthesising because it uses up all the carbon dioxide. Explain what will actually happen and why the claim is only partly right. · 4 marks · Complete the summary of photosynthesis. Each gap is marked as a whole answer, and the word bank contains more words than gaps. · 4 marks · Photosynthesis takes in ________ (1) from the air and ________ (2) from the soil. It happens in the ________ (3), where chlorophyll absorbs light. The plant makes ________ (4) and releases ________ (5). · 1. Gas taken in from the air · 2. Reactant taken in from the soil · 3. Organelle where photosynthesis happens · 4. Carbohydrate product · 5. Gas released · Word bank: carbon dioxide · water · chloroplast · glucose · oxygen · nitrogen · mitochondrion · Match each structure or substance to the job it does in photosynthesis. · 4 marks · Structure or substance	Answer letter	Job in photosynthesis · 1. Chlorophyll		A. Absorbs light energy · 2. Stomata		B. The carbohydrate product used for respiration or stored as starch · 3. Chloroplast		C. Transports water to the leaf · 4. Xylem		D. Lets carbon dioxide enter the leaf · 5. Glucose		E. The organelle where photosynthesis takes place · A rate-versus-light-intensity graph rises steeply at low light and then becomes flat at 12 mm³ of oxygen per minute above 20 arbitrary units of light. State which factor limits the rate above 20 units, and explain why adding more light does not increase it. · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · A lake has become cloudy because of algal growth near the surface. Plants living on the lake bed, several metres down, are dying. Use the limiting-factor idea to explain why, and suggest why adding nutrients to the lake could make the problem worse rather than better. · The setting is an ecosystem rather than a leaf, and the causal chain runs through light penetration, photosynthesis on the lake bed and competition at the surface. The learner must apply the same limiting-factor reasoning without a graph or a labelled diagram. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Name the reactants and products of photosynthesis and the organelle where it happens. (next day) · Why does raising the temperature of a photosynthesising plant increase the rate up to a point and then decrease it sharply? (week later) · A plant is kept in the dark for two days. Explain why its leaves still produce carbon dioxide. (month later) · Summary · Photosynthesis uses light energy to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the chloroplast. · The rate is set by whichever factor is in shortest supply; a plateau means the limiting factor has changed. · Plants respire continuously as well as photosynthesising, so gas exchange is a net effect of two rates. · Structure serves function: chloroplast density, stomata and air spaces all exist to make the process efficient. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Acids, bases & salts · chemistry · GCSE Chemistry, acids, bases and salts: proton transfer, pH, neutralisation, strong and weak acids · Key Stage 3 to GCSE · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Classify an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor, and distinguish an alkali from a base. · You will show this by: Given ammonia, sodium hydroxide and calcium carbonate, the learner places each on the acid–base axis and explains the classification by what accepts H⁺, not by whether the formula contains OH. · Interpret pH as a logarithmic measure of H⁺ concentration and calculate the effect of a tenfold dilution. · You will show this by: The learner states that pH 3 has one hundred times the H⁺ concentration of pH 5, and that diluting a strong acid tenfold raises its pH by one unit, not by a factor of ten. · Predict the salt from an acid–base reaction, write a balanced equation, and separate strong from concentrated using ionisation and conductivity evidence. · You will show this by: The learner writes a balanced equation for sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide, identifies the spectator ions, and explains why 0.1 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid is a weaker conductor than 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. · Before you start · Hydrogen chloride has the formula HCl. What does that formula tell you about the ratio of atoms, and what does it not tell you about how the substance behaves in water? · Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but a sodium chloride solution does. Explain the difference. · Why this matters · Lemon juice, vinegar and the acid in your stomach share a property that has nothing to do with how dangerous they look: they can donate a hydrogen ion. Soap and bleach feel slippery for a different reason — they are alkaline. A swimming pool can be clear and still sting your eyes because its pH is wrong, and a bottle labelled 'strong acid' can be less acidic than a concentrated weak acid if it is very dilute. · Proton transfer explains why an antacid settles a stomach, why limestone raises the pH of a lake, and why a titration can find an unknown concentration. The pH scale compresses a huge range of H⁺ concentrations into small numbers, which is useful only if you remember that each step is a factor of ten. And the distinction between strong and concentrated is a safety distinction as well as a chemical one: it tells you whether the danger comes from complete ionisation or from how much acid is present. · The explanation · An acid donates a proton; a base accepts one · In aqueous solution, an acid releases hydrogen ions, H⁺. A hydrogen ion is a proton, so the modern definition is broader than 'contains H': an acid is a proton donor. Hydrogen chloride ionises completely in water, HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, and nitric acid behaves in the same way. A base is a proton acceptor. Hydroxide ions accept H⁺ to form water, OH⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O, which is why soluble hydroxides such as sodium hydroxide are alkaline. Ammonia is also a base: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, even though its formula contains no OH. · An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis: copper(II) oxide and calcium carbonate are bases that do not dissolve to give an alkaline solution. Bases do not have to contain hydroxide either. Metal oxides, hydroxides and carbonates all accept protons, and the reaction with an acid produces a salt. Keeping the definition at the level of proton transfer stops the formula from being treated as the definition. · pH is logarithmic, so one unit is a factor of ten · At 25 °C, a neutral aqueous solution has pH 7. Values below 7 are acidic and values above 7 are alkaline. The number is not a linear amount of acid: pH is defined as −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the concentration of hydrogen ions in mol dm⁻³. A solution of pH 3 therefore has 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ of H⁺, and a solution of pH 5 has 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. pH 3 is one hundred times more concentrated in H⁺ than pH 5, because the difference of two pH units corresponds to two factors of ten. · This is why pH 0 does not mean 'no acid' and pH 14 does not mean 'the most dangerous substance'. It also explains why a dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid: pH measures the H⁺ that is actually free in solution, not the amount of acid put into the bottle. Universal indicator gives an approximate colour, while a calibrated pH meter gives a number. At temperatures other than 25 °C the neutral pH is not exactly 7, so 'neutral' is defined by equal H⁺ and OH⁻ concentrations, not by the number alone. · Neutralisation transfers a proton and leaves a salt · An acid reacting with a hydroxide base produces a salt and water: acid + base → salt + water. The cation of the salt comes from the base and the anion comes from the acid. Hydrochloric acid gives chloride salts, sulfuric acid gives sulfates, nitric acid gives nitrates, and ethanoic acid gives ethanoates. The balanced equation must respect the charges as well as the atoms: sulfuric acid has two protons to donate, so it needs two hydroxide ions, as in H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. · The essential change is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. Sodium and sulfate ions are spectators: they are present before and after and do not change. Metal oxides and carbonates are also bases, but they do not fit the simple 'salt + water' pattern: a carbonate also releases carbon dioxide, as in 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. A neutralisation reaction is not the same as a neutral solution. The mixture is at pH 7 only when the acid and base have reacted in exactly the right proportions and both are strong; a weak acid with a strong base can leave an alkaline solution at the equivalence point. · Strong and concentrated are independent axes · Strong describes how completely an acid ionises in water. Hydrochloric and nitric acids are strong: essentially every molecule donates its proton. Ethanoic acid is weak: only a small fraction of its molecules ionise, so the solution contains mostly intact molecules and relatively few H⁺ ions. Concentrated describes how much acid is dissolved per unit volume. It says nothing about the fraction that ionises. A solution can be strong and dilute, strong and concentrated, weak and dilute, or weak and concentrated. · The evidence separates the two ideas. At the same concentration, the strong acid has more mobile ions, so its solution conducts electricity better and usually has a lower pH. A weak acid can be made more concentrated and become more acidic, but it is still weak: dilution does not turn a strong acid weak, and concentration does not turn a weak acid strong. When a label says 'strong', ask what is fully ionised; when it says 'concentrated', ask how much is present per litre. A hazard assessment needs both, along with the actual pH. · Diagrams and representations · Hydrochloric acid neutralises sodium hydroxide. The sodium and chloride ions are spectators; the proton and hydroxide ion combine to form water. · HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O   ·   H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O · The full equation accounts for every ion. The ionic equation shows only the species that change. Neither equation says the final solution is neutral: that depends on the amounts mixed. · Two solutions of the same concentration. Hydrochloric acid is fully ionised, so it supplies many H⁺ ions and conducts well. Ethanoic acid is only partly ionised, so most of its molecules remain intact, fewer H⁺ ions are free, and the solution conducts less. · 0.1 mol dm⁻³ HCl: fully ionised, pH ≈ 1   ·   0.1 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH: partly ionised, pH ≈ 3 · The difference is the fraction ionised, not the amount dissolved. Both solutions are 0.1 mol dm⁻³, so concentration is held constant while strength changes. · Diluting a strong acid by a known factor lowers the H⁺ concentration by that factor. Because pH is logarithmic, a tenfold dilution raises the pH by one unit; a hundredfold dilution raises it by two. · pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]   ·   10 cm³ of pH 2 diluted to 1000 cm³ is a 100-fold dilution, so pH 2 → pH 4 · This calculation assumes the acid is strong and the dilution is well above the point where water's own ionisation matters. Near pH 7, adding water cannot simply be treated as another factor of ten. · The acid's anion names the salt family. The base's cation names the first part of the salt. Charges decide how many of each ion are needed, so the formula is built from the ions rather than copied from the acid. · HCl → chloride   ·   H₂SO₄ → sulfate   ·   HNO₃ → nitrate   ·   CH₃COOH → ethanoate · Sulfuric acid can donate two protons, so a sulfate salt needs two singly charged cations: KOH gives K₂SO₄, while NaOH gives Na₂SO₄. · Worked examples · Write the balanced equation and the ionic equation for the reaction between sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide. · Identify the ions: H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ from the acid; K⁺ and OH⁻ from the base. · Why: Sulfuric acid can donate two protons, so its anion carries a 2− charge. Potassium hydroxide supplies one K⁺ for every OH⁻. Writing the ions first prevents the formula being assembled by guesswork. · Combine one sulfate ion with two potassium ions, and balance the proton transfer with two hydroxide ions: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. · Why: The two negative charges on sulfate need two positive potassium ions. The two H⁺ from sulfuric acid need two OH⁻ to become two water molecules. Every atom and every charge now balances. · Remove the spectator ions to obtain H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. · Why: Potassium and sulfate ions appear unchanged on both sides. The ionic equation keeps the reaction that actually happens and shows why every acid–hydroxide neutralisation has the same core. · Answer: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O; the ionic equation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, with K⁺ and SO₄²⁻ as spectators. · 10 cm³ of a strong acid solution of pH 2 is diluted with pure water to a final volume of 1000 cm³. Calculate the new pH. · Find the dilution factor: 1000 ÷ 10 = 100. · Why: The same amount of acid is spread through a hundred times the volume, so its concentration falls by a factor of one hundred. The dilution factor is a ratio of volumes, not a subtraction. · Reduce the H⁺ concentration by that factor: from 10⁻² to 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³. · Why: pH 2 means [H⁺] = 10⁻². Dividing by 100 subtracts two from the exponent, giving 10⁻⁴. The acid is strong, so the H⁺ concentration is taken as the acid's concentration for this school-level calculation. · Convert back to pH: −log₁₀(10⁻⁴) = 4. · Why: Each factor of ten changes pH by one unit, and there were two factors of ten, so the pH rises by two. The answer is pH 4, not pH 200 or pH 7: dilution lowers concentration but does not remove every acid particle. · Answer: The new pH is 4. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: A strong acid is the same thing as a concentrated acid. · Why it fails: Strength is the fraction of acid molecules that ionise; concentration is how many moles are dissolved per litre. A 0.001 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid solution is strong because it is fully ionised, but it is very dilute and has pH 3. A concentrated ethanoic acid solution can have a lower pH than that while remaining weak. The two words answer different questions. · Correct reasoning: Describe both axes separately: 'strong' means fully ionised, 'concentrated' means a large amount per litre. Then quote the pH or the concentration as evidence rather than using either word as a substitute for the other. · Wrong: it is strong, so it must be concentrated and dangerous · Right: it is strong because it fully ionises, but at this dilution its pH is only 3 · Wrong belief: pH is a linear amount, so pH 4 is twice as acidic as pH 2. · Why it fails: The pH scale is logarithmic. pH 2 means [H⁺] = 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ and pH 4 means 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, so pH 2 has one hundred times the H⁺ concentration of pH 4, not twice. Reversing the comparison is just as wrong: the lower pH is the more acidic solution. · Correct reasoning: Turn each pH into a power of ten before comparing. A difference of one pH unit is a factor of ten in H⁺ concentration; a difference of two units is a factor of one hundred. · Wrong: pH 4 is twice pH 2 · Right: pH 2 has 100 times the H⁺ concentration of pH 4 · Wrong belief: Every base contains OH⁻, and every neutralisation leaves a neutral solution. · Why it fails: Ammonia is a base because it accepts H⁺ to form NH₄⁺, even though it contains no hydroxide. A base is defined by proton acceptance, and an alkali is simply a base that dissolves. Separately, a neutralisation reaction can leave an acidic or alkaline solution if the amounts are not at the equivalence point, or if a weak acid is mixed with a strong base. · Correct reasoning: Classify bases by what they do to H⁺, not by whether OH appears in the formula. Treat 'neutralisation' as the reaction and 'neutral' as a statement about the final pH; test the result rather than assuming it. · Wrong: ammonia cannot be a base because it has no OH, and all neutralisations end at pH 7 · Right: ammonia accepts H⁺, so it is a base; the final pH depends on the amounts and the acid–base pair · Guided practice · Ammonia solution turns universal indicator blue and reacts with hydrochloric acid to form ammonium chloride. Is ammonia an acid, a base or an alkali? Explain using proton transfer. · Hint: Look at what ammonia does to H⁺. Does it donate a proton or accept one? Then decide whether it is soluble. · Write the balanced equation for the reaction between nitric acid and calcium hydroxide, and name the salt formed. · Hint: Calcium ions have a 2+ charge and nitrate has a 1− charge, so two nitrate ions are needed. Balance the protons with two hydroxide ions. · A strong acid solution has pH 2. It is diluted tenfold. Calculate the new pH and explain why it is not pH 20. · Hint: Tenfold dilution divides [H⁺] by ten. What does that do to the exponent in 10⁻²? · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 12 marks. · A learner says: 'The 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is stronger and more concentrated than the 0.1 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid, so of course it has the lower pH.' Which parts of this statement are right, and which are wrong? Explain using ionisation. · 4 marks · A strong acid solution has pH 3. It is diluted with pure water until its volume is 100 times greater. Calculate the new pH. · 4 marks · Name the salt formed when sulfuric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide. · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · A lake has become acidic at pH 4.5 because of acid rain. An engineer proposes adding water from a nearby river to raise the pH. Explain why dilution is a poor way to solve the problem, and why adding powdered limestone (calcium carbonate) is more effective. Include the ionic equation for the reaction that removes H⁺. · The lesson develops pH as a logarithmic scale and neutralisation as proton transfer. Here the learner must apply both to an environmental decision, compare dilution with chemical removal, and write the proton-transfer equation for a carbonate rather than a hydroxide. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Define an acid, a base and an alkali in one sentence each. (next day) · How many times greater is the H⁺ concentration at pH 3 than at pH 6? (week later) · Why does 0.1 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid conduct electricity less well than 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid? (month later) · Summary · An acid donates a proton; a base accepts one. An alkali is a soluble base, and bases do not have to contain OH⁻. · pH is logarithmic: one unit is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration, and 7 is neutral only at 25 °C. · Neutralisation is proton transfer to water; the acid's anion names the salt, and spectator ions are removed from the ionic equation. · Strength is the degree of ionisation; concentration is the amount per litre. Equal concentrations do not mean equal pH. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Rates of reaction · chemistry · GCSE Chemistry, rates of reaction: measuring rate, collision theory, temperature, concentration, surface area, catalysts and rate graphs · Key Stage 3 to GCSE · version 1.1.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Calculate a mean rate from a measured change and a time interval, and state the unit that makes the number a rate. · You will show this by: Given 72 cm³ of gas collected in 3.0 minutes, the learner reports 0.40 cm³/s, shows the division by 180 seconds, and explains why 72 cm³ alone is an amount rather than a rate. · Use collision theory to explain how temperature, concentration or pressure, and surface area change the rate of a reaction. · You will show this by: For a reaction between marble chips and acid, the learner explains that powdering increases the exposed surface and therefore the frequency of collisions, without claiming that the activation energy has changed. · Explain what a catalyst does to the activation energy and the rate, and what it does not change. · You will show this by: The learner states that a catalyst provides an alternative route with lower activation energy, is not used up, and does not change the final amount or the equilibrium position of a reversible reaction. · Interpret a rate graph, distinguishing the initial rate from a later mean rate and explaining a plateau. · You will show this by: On a graph of gas volume against time, the learner identifies the steepest gradient at the start, calculates a mean rate over a stated interval, and explains that the plateau occurs when a reactant has been used up. · Before you start · A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen releases a large amount of energy when it reacts, yet it can sit at room temperature without reacting. What must the molecules do before the reaction can start? · What is activation energy, and why is it a barrier rather than the overall energy change of the reaction? · Why this matters · A glow stick is brightest in the first minute and dim after an hour. The same amount of chemical is in the tube at both times, but the light-producing reaction is faster at the start. A marble chip dropped into acid fizzes slowly; the same mass of powdered marble in the same acid fizzes vigorously. Neither change is a change in what the products are. Both are changes in how quickly the reactants become products. · Rates matter outside the laboratory. A medicine has to act quickly enough to help and slowly enough to last; a fuel has to burn at a controlled speed; food spoils faster in warmth because the reactions that break it down speed up. Collision theory explains all of those cases with one picture: particles must meet, and the meeting must have enough energy. Once a learner can separate the frequency of collisions from the fraction that succeeds, temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts stop being four facts to memorise. · The explanation · A rate is a change divided by the time it took · Rate answers the question “how much change in how long?”. If 72 cm³ of gas is collected in 3.0 minutes, the mean rate is 72 cm³ ÷ 180 s = 0.40 cm³/s. The unit is part of the answer because it says what changed and what the change was measured against. A volume, a mass or a concentration on its own is an amount; dividing by time turns it into a rate. · A mean rate over a long interval hides the shape of the reaction. Most reactions are fastest at the beginning, when the reactants are most concentrated, and slow down as they are used up. The initial rate is the gradient at the very start of the graph, before the concentration has fallen much. A later mean rate is the gradient of a chord drawn between two times. Both are legitimate measurements, but they answer different questions and should not be reported as the same number. · A rate graph also shows when a reaction has stopped. The curve flattens when a reactant is used up, not because the particles have stopped moving. Adding more of the limiting reactant can restart the reaction; adding more of an excess reactant cannot, because the other reactant is already gone. The plateau is therefore evidence about amount, while the slope before it is evidence about speed. · Collisions must happen, and they must be energetic enough · For a reaction to occur, reactant particles must collide. Not every collision produces products: the particles must be oriented so that the reacting parts meet, and together they must have at least the activation energy needed to break the bonds that must break. Collision theory separates the rate into two factors: how often collisions occur, and what fraction of those collisions has enough energy. Anything that raises either factor raises the rate. · Concentration is the number of particles in a given volume. A more concentrated solution has more reactant particles in the same space, so collisions are more frequent and the rate is higher. Increasing the pressure of a gas has a similar effect because it squeezes the same number of particles into a smaller volume. The particles do not become more energetic; there are simply more opportunities for them to meet. · Surface area matters when one reactant is a solid. A reaction can happen only at the exposed surface, where the solid meets the solution or gas. Breaking a lump into smaller pieces exposes more surface for the same mass, so collisions between the solid and the other reactant are more frequent. The activation energy has not changed. A powder is not “more reactive” in the sense of a different chemistry; it simply offers more places for the reaction to occur. · Temperature changes both the frequency and the success fraction · Heating a reaction makes the particles move faster on average. Faster particles collide more often, which raises the collision frequency. Temperature also changes the distribution of kinetic energy: a larger fraction of collisions now has at least the activation energy, so a larger fraction of meetings succeeds. Both effects point the same way, which is why a modest temperature rise can produce a large increase in rate. · It is not accurate to say that heat “makes the particles expand” or “gives the reaction more energy” in a vague sense. The particles have a distribution of energies at any temperature; heating shifts that distribution toward higher energies. The activation barrier stays where it is. More particles can clear it, rather than each particle receiving a fixed extra amount. · Temperature can do something the other levers cannot: in a reversible reaction it can change the equilibrium position, because the forward and reverse reactions do not usually have the same activation energy. Concentration, pressure and surface area change how quickly equilibrium is reached, but they do not change the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature. A rate answer should say which effect is being claimed. · A catalyst lowers the barrier without being used up · A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. With a lower hill to climb, a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy to react, so the rate increases. The catalyst is not consumed by the overall reaction: it takes part in one step and is regenerated in another, so a small amount can catalyse a large amount of reaction. It does not become a product, and it does not change the balanced equation. · A catalyst does not change the energy of the reactants or the products, so it does not change the overall energy change. In a reversible reaction it lowers the barrier for both the forward and reverse directions, so equilibrium is reached sooner but is not pushed to one side. This is why a catalyst can make a process faster and cheaper without increasing the yield at equilibrium — a distinction that matters in industrial chemistry. · Enzymes are biological catalysts. Their specificity comes from shape: a substrate fits a region of the enzyme, and the enzyme holds it in the orientation that makes the reaction easier. High temperature or the wrong pH can change that shape and stop the catalysis, which is why an enzyme has an optimum rather than a simple “hotter is always faster” rule. The same collision-theory language applies, with the shape of the catalyst adding a condition. · Read the gradient, then read the plateau · A rate graph is a record of amount against time. Its gradient at any point is the rate at that moment. The gradient is steepest at the beginning, when the reactant concentration is highest, and becomes shallower as the reactant is consumed. If the graph is a straight line, the rate is constant over that interval; if it curves, the rate is changing. A mean rate is a chord, while an instantaneous rate is a tangent. · The end of the graph is just as informative. When the curve becomes flat, the amount of product is no longer changing, so the rate has fallen to an unmeasurably small value. In a closed system with a limiting reactant, this usually means that reactant has been used up. If the same reaction is repeated with twice as much of the limiting reactant, the plateau will generally be higher because more product can form; if the other reactant is in excess, adding more of it may not change the final amount. · The choice of measurement is part of the method. Gas volume is convenient when a gas is produced; mass loss is convenient when a gas escapes from an open flask; colour or turbidity is convenient when a visible change occurs. Each method has a limit. A colour change may be hard to time precisely, and a mass loss may be too small early in the reaction. The best method is the one that changes clearly over the interval being measured. · Diagrams and representations · The reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen gas, so the volume of gas collected is a direct observable of how far the reaction has gone. · Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ · The equation is balanced: one magnesium, two hydrogen and two chlorine atoms on each side. The gas volume rises as H₂ is produced, and the rate is the change in that volume divided by the time. · Reactant particles move through the mixture and collide. A collision can succeed only when the particles have at least the activation energy and meet in a suitable orientation. Increasing concentration increases the number of collisions; heating increases both the number and the fraction that succeed. · rate = collision frequency × fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Eₐ · The equation is a summary, not a calculation to memorise. Surface area changes the exposed area where collisions can occur; a catalyst lowers Eₐ and therefore raises the successful fraction. · Mean rate is found by dividing the measured change by the time interval. The units must be converted to a consistent time unit before dividing, and the answer carries the unit of the change divided by the unit of time. · mean rate = change in amount ÷ time taken · For 48 cm³ in 2.0 minutes: 2.0 minutes is 120 s, so the mean rate is 48 ÷ 120 = 0.40 cm³/s. A rate is not the same as the total volume collected. · A catalyst offers a different route between the same reactants and products. The new route has a lower peak, so more collisions have enough energy to cross it, but the starting and finishing levels are unchanged. · uncatalysed route: higher Eₐ   ·   catalysed route: lower Eₐ   ·   reactants and products unchanged · The catalyst is regenerated at the end of the route. It changes the rate and the time needed to reach equilibrium, not the final position or the overall energy change. · Worked examples · In an experiment, 0.080 g of magnesium ribbon reacts with excess hydrochloric acid. The mass loss after 20.0 s is 0.080 g. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss in g/s and explain why the instantaneous rate at the start is higher. · Write the mean rate as the mass change divided by the time interval: 0.080 g ÷ 20.0 s. · Why: A mean rate needs both the amount that changed and the time over which it changed; dividing by time is what turns the mass into a rate. · Carry out the division: 0.080 ÷ 20.0 = 0.0040 g/s. · Why: The unit is grams per second because the numerator is in grams and the denominator is in seconds; quoting only 0.0040 would hide what was measured. · State that the instantaneous rate at the start is higher because the acid concentration is highest then. · Why: More acid particles per unit volume means more frequent collisions between the acid and the magnesium surface, so the initial gradient is steeper than the mean over the whole interval. · Distinguish the plateau from a change in the particles' speed. · Why: When the magnesium is used up, the mass stops changing even though the particles continue to move; the flat graph is evidence that the limiting reactant has been consumed, not that motion has stopped. · Answer: Mean rate = 0.080 g ÷ 20.0 s = 0.0040 g/s. The initial rate is higher because the acid is most concentrated at the start, so collisions with the metal surface are more frequent. The rate then falls as the acid is used up, and the mass becomes constant when the magnesium is exhausted. · Two experiments use 2.0 g of calcium carbonate and 25 cm³ of the same hydrochloric acid at the same temperature. Experiment A uses one large chip; Experiment B uses the same mass of powder. Experiment A collects 40 cm³ of gas in 60 s; Experiment B collects 40 cm³ in 15 s. Calculate both mean rates and explain the difference. · Calculate the mean rate for the chip: 40 cm³ ÷ 60 s = 0.67 cm³/s. · Why: The volume of gas collected is divided by the time taken, giving a rate in cubic centimetres per second for this experiment. · Calculate the mean rate for the powder: 40 cm³ ÷ 15 s = 2.7 cm³/s. · Why: The same volume is produced in a quarter of the time, so the powder's mean rate is about four times larger. · Explain the difference using exposed surface area rather than a different activation energy. · Why: The powder has a much larger surface in contact with the acid, so acid particles collide with the solid more frequently; the activation energy for the reaction itself is unchanged. · Check that the final volume can still be the same. · Why: Both experiments use the same mass of calcium carbonate, so they can produce the same maximum volume of gas; the powder simply reaches that limit sooner. · Answer: Chip mean rate = 40 ÷ 60 = 0.67 cm³/s. Powder mean rate = 40 ÷ 15 = 2.7 cm³/s (both to two significant figures). The powder is faster because the same mass has a much larger exposed surface area, so collisions between acid particles and the solid are more frequent. The final volume is the same because the amount of calcium carbonate is the same. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: A catalyst increases the yield of a reversible reaction. · Why it fails: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions, so equilibrium is reached sooner. It does not change the energy of the reactants or the products, so it does not move the equilibrium position or change the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature. The final amount at equilibrium is controlled by the conditions, not by how quickly the mixture gets there. · Correct reasoning: Separate rate from position: a catalyst changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, while temperature, pressure and concentration change where the equilibrium lies. A catalyst can raise the yield per unit time without raising the yield at equilibrium. · Wrong: the catalyst pushes the reaction to the products, so there is more product at equilibrium · Right: the catalyst helps both directions reach equilibrium sooner, but the equilibrium amount is unchanged · Wrong belief: Heating a reaction makes the particles expand, so there is more space for them to react. · Why it fails: Particles do not expand in the way this explanation suggests. Heating increases their average kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more often. It also shifts the distribution of energies so that a larger fraction of collisions has at least the activation energy. The barrier itself does not move. · Correct reasoning: Explain temperature with collision frequency and the fraction of collisions that clear Eₐ. In a gas, heating can also change the volume or pressure, but that is a separate effect on concentration. · Wrong: the particles get bigger and spread out, so the reaction has more room · Right: the particles move faster and more of them have enough energy to clear the activation barrier · Wrong belief: A rate is the amount of product formed. · Why it fails: The amount of product is a quantity, not a speed. A reaction can make a large amount slowly or a small amount quickly. Rate is the change in amount divided by the time, so the same final volume can be produced at a high rate or a low rate. Reporting only the volume loses the time information that makes it a rate. · Correct reasoning: Always write the division by time and the unit. If a question asks for a rate, the answer needs a per-second, per-minute or per-unit-time form; if it asks for the amount, it does not. · Wrong: the rate is 40 cm³ because that is how much gas was collected · Right: the rate is 40 cm³ ÷ 60 s = 0.67 cm³/s; 40 cm³ is the amount collected · Wrong belief: Powdering a solid makes it more reactive by lowering its activation energy. · Why it fails: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases the exposed surface area. More surface means more frequent collisions between the solid and the other reactant, so the rate rises. The activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway, not of the particle size, and it is unchanged by powdering. · Correct reasoning: Use surface area to explain the change in collision frequency. Use a catalyst to explain a change in activation energy. The two explanations both raise the rate, but they are not the same mechanism. · Wrong: the powder has a lower activation energy, so it reacts faster · Right: the powder exposes more surface, so collisions are more frequent; the activation energy is the same · Guided practice · A reaction collects 72 cm³ of gas in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the mean rate in cm³/s. · Hint: Convert the time to seconds first, then divide the volume by that time; the unit of the answer comes from the division. · A reaction starts quickly and then slows down. Explain why the rate falls even though the temperature is kept constant. · Hint: Think about what happens to the concentration of the reactants as the reaction proceeds, and what that does to the frequency of collisions. · A catalyst makes a reaction faster, but the final volume of gas collected is the same. Explain why the volume is unchanged. · Hint: Ask what the catalyst changes about the pathway and what it leaves unchanged about the reactants and products. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 20 marks. · In an experiment, 0.10 g of magnesium reacts with excess acid and the mass loss after 25 s is 0.10 g. Calculate the mean rate of mass loss in g/s. · 4 marks · A reaction collects 48 cm³ of gas in 2.0 minutes. Calculate the mean rate in cm³/s. · 4 marks · A reaction is repeated with the same amounts at the same temperature, once with a catalyst and once without. Explain why the catalysed reaction reaches the same final amount of product sooner. · 4 marks · A student plans an experiment to measure how halving the concentration of hydrochloric acid changes the rate of reaction with magnesium ribbon. Describe how the gas volume should be measured over time, state two variables that must be controlled, and explain how a mean rate is obtained from the graph. · 4 marks · A graph of gas volume against time rises from 0 to 40 cm³ in the first 20 s, reaches 72 cm³ at 60 s and levels at 80 cm³ after 90 s. Calculate the initial rate and the mean rate over 90 s, and explain why the graph flattens. · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · A glow stick is bright for the first minute and then becomes dim over several hours. A second glow stick is placed in a freezer and glows dimly for much longer. Explain both observations using collision theory and the idea of a rate, rather than saying that the chemical “runs out”. Both sticks contain the same amounts. · The lesson measured gas volume from a reaction in a flask. Here the observable is light, the reaction is the same in both sticks, and the learner must transfer the rate explanation to a different measurement and a different temperature without inventing a new chemical reaction. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · State the two conditions collision theory requires for a collision to produce a reaction. (next day) · A reaction collects 120 cm³ of gas in 4.0 minutes. Calculate the mean rate in cm³/s. (week later) · Explain the difference between what a catalyst changes and what it does not change in a reversible reaction. (month later) · Summary · Rate is a change in amount divided by time; the unit is part of the answer, and a mean rate over a long interval is not the initial rate. · Collision theory requires collisions with enough energy and a suitable orientation; concentration and surface area change collision frequency, while a catalyst changes the fraction that clears the barrier. · Heating increases both collision frequency and the fraction of collisions with at least the activation energy; it can also change an equilibrium position in a reversible reaction. · A rate graph's gradient is the rate, its steep start is the highest concentration, and its plateau is evidence that a limiting reactant has been used up. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Circuits · physics · GCSE Physics, electricity: current, potential difference and resistance · Key Stage 3 to GCSE · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Use the relationship between potential difference, current and resistance to find any one of the three when the other two are known. · You will show this by: Given a twelve volt supply driving three amps, the learner rearranges to resistance equals voltage divided by current and answers four ohms, with the unit. · Predict whether current or potential difference is shared in a series and in a parallel circuit, and justify the prediction from conservation. · You will show this by: The learner says the current is the same at every point in a series loop because charge cannot pile up, and that the potential differences add because energy per coulomb is transferred in stages. · Explain why adding a second bulb in parallel makes each bulb as bright as before, while adding it in series dims both. · You will show this by: The learner attributes the parallel case to each branch having the full supply voltage, and the series case to the supply voltage being shared between two resistances. · Before you start · What does a battery do to the charge that flows through it? · A torch uses twenty joules of energy in four seconds. What is its power, and what does the number mean? · Why this matters · Two identical bulbs, one battery. Wire them one after the other and both look dim. Wire them side by side, each with its own path back to the battery, and both look as bright as a single bulb on its own. · The bulbs did not change and the battery did not change, so the difference must be in what each bulb is given. A circuit is an energy story told in two currencies: charge, which flows and is never used up, and energy per charge, which is transferred and is used up. Keeping those two separate is the whole of this topic. · The explanation · Current is charge passing, not charge consumed · Current is the rate at which charge passes a point, measured in amperes: one amp is one coulomb each second. Charge is conserved, so in a single loop the same charge passes every point in the same time. The current is therefore the same before the bulb, inside the bulb and after it. A bulb does not use up current; it transfers energy from the charge that passes through it. · This is why an ammeter reads the same value anywhere in a series circuit, and why the readings either side of a component are not 'before and after'. If current were consumed, charge would accumulate inside the bulb, and nothing in the physics allows that. · Potential difference is energy per charge, and it is what gets shared · The battery gives each coulomb a certain amount of energy. As charge passes through a component, some of that energy is transferred to the surroundings — as light and heat in a bulb. The potential difference across the component is the energy transferred per coulomb passing through it, measured in volts: one volt is one joule per coulomb. · In a series loop the charge passes through every component in turn, so the energy per coulomb is handed out in stages and the potential differences add to the supply voltage. In a parallel circuit each branch connects directly across the supply, so every branch gets the full energy per coulomb and the potential difference across each branch equals the supply voltage. The current then divides between the branches, because the same total charge per second has more than one route. · Resistance is the opposition that sets the current · For a component at constant temperature, the current through it is proportional to the potential difference across it. The constant of proportionality is the resistance: potential difference equals current times resistance, with resistance in ohms. Rearranging is the everyday skill — resistance is voltage divided by current, and current is voltage divided by resistance. · The relationship assumes the temperature stays constant. A filament bulb heats up, its resistance rises, and the graph of current against voltage curves rather than staying straight. Naming that assumption is part of using the equation honestly, and a thermistor or a diode breaks it in a different direction on purpose. · Series and parallel are consequences, not conventions · In series there is one path, so the current has nowhere else to go and is the same throughout; the resistances add because the charge is pushed through each obstacle in turn. In parallel there are several paths, so the current splits; the total resistance falls because adding a path makes it easier for charge to flow, which is why a parallel circuit draws more current from the same supply. · Both rules come from the same two conservation statements: charge is conserved at a junction, and energy per coulomb is conserved around a loop. A learner who can derive the rules from those statements can answer a circuit question they have not seen; a learner who has memorised 'series adds' will meet a combination circuit and have nothing to fall back on. · Diagrams and representations · The relationship between potential difference, current and resistance. Rearrange before substituting, so the quantity you want is alone on the left. · V = I R · V is the potential difference in volts, I the current in amperes and R the resistance in ohms. The equation holds for a component at constant temperature. · Each symbol is a quantity with a unit, and the unit is what makes an answer checkable. · V in volts (V) · I in amperes (A) · R in ohms (Ω) · P in watts (W) · An answer of four is not an answer. Four ohms is, and four volts would be a different physical claim entirely. · Two circuits side by side. In the series circuit one path runs through both bulbs, so the same current passes each and the supply voltage divides between them. In the parallel circuit each bulb has its own branch across the supply, so each branch has the full supply voltage and the current divides. · series: one path · parallel: two branches across the same supply · The arrows matter. In series the current arrow has one route; in parallel it splits at the junction and rejoins. The voltage label is written across each branch, not across the whole circuit. · Current against potential difference for a fixed resistor and for a filament bulb. The resistor gives a straight line through the origin; the bulb curves as it heats and its resistance rises. · resistor: straight through origin · bulb: curve steepening then flattening · The gradient of the straight line is one over the resistance. The curve is not a mistake: the assumption of constant temperature has stopped holding. · Worked examples · A twelve volt supply drives a current of three amps through a resistor. Find its resistance. · Write the equation and rearrange it for the quantity asked for: R = V / I. · Why: The question gives V and I and asks for R, so R must be alone on one side before any numbers go in. Substituting first and rearranging afterwards is where sign and division errors enter. · Substitute the values: R = 12 / 3. · Why: Twelve volts and three amps are in the correct units already, so no conversion is needed. Writing the units beside the numbers keeps track of what the division means. · Calculate and state the unit: R = 4 Ω. · Why: Volts divided by amps gives ohms. A bare four would not say whether it was four ohms, four volts or four amps. · Answer: 4 Ω · Two six ohm resistors are connected in series across a twelve volt supply. Find the current through the circuit and the potential difference across each resistor. · Find the total resistance: R = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. · Why: In series the charge passes through both resistors in turn, so the two obstacles add. The same current flows through each. · Rearrange V = I R for current: I = V / R = 12 / 12. · Why: The supply voltage acts across the whole series combination, so the total resistance is the correct denominator for the total current. · Calculate: I = 1 A, and then find each potential difference with V = I R = 1 × 6. · Why: The current is the same through both resistors, so each takes one amp. Each potential difference is therefore six volts, and the two add to the twelve volt supply, which is the check that the energy bookkeeping is consistent. · Answer: 1 A, with 6 V across each resistor · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: Current is used up as it goes round the circuit, so the bulb uses some of it. · Why it fails: Charge is conserved. If a bulb consumed current, charge would have to accumulate inside it, and there is nothing in the physics that allows that. What the bulb takes is energy, not charge, so the current after the bulb is the same as the current before it. · Correct reasoning: Separate the two currencies. Charge flows round the loop and is never consumed; energy per charge is transferred at each component. The ammeter reading is the same everywhere in a series loop, and the voltmeter reading is what changes. · Wrong: the current after the bulb is smaller because the bulb used some up · Right: the current is the same; the bulb transferred energy from the charge passing through it · Wrong belief: The voltage is the same everywhere in a series circuit. · Why it fails: Potential difference is energy transferred per coulomb, and in a series loop each coulomb passes through every component in turn. If every component took the full supply voltage, the charge would gain energy it was never given. The potential differences must add to the supply voltage. · Correct reasoning: In series the current is shared (it is the same everywhere) and the potential differences add. In parallel the potential difference is shared (it is the same across every branch) and the currents add. The two rules are mirror images. · Wrong: series: 12 V across each of two bulbs · Right: series: 6 V across each of two equal bulbs, adding to 12 V · Wrong belief: Adding a second bulb in parallel makes the circuit harder to push current through, so both bulbs dim. · Why it fails: Adding a parallel branch gives the charge another route, which makes it easier to flow, not harder. The total resistance falls and the supply delivers more current. Each branch still sits directly across the supply, so each bulb keeps the full voltage and stays as bright as it was alone. · Correct reasoning: In series the resistances add and every component shares the voltage, so both dim. In parallel the branches each see the full supply voltage, so brightness is unchanged and the battery supplies more total current. · Wrong: parallel: two bulbs share 12 V, so each gets 6 V · Right: parallel: each branch gets 12 V and the currents add · Guided practice · A resistor of resistance eight ohms carries a current of two amps. What is the potential difference across it? · Hint: You are asked for V, and the equation already has V alone on the left. · Three identical bulbs are connected in series to a twelve volt supply. What is the potential difference across each bulb, and what current flows if each has resistance four ohms? · Hint: The supply voltage is shared equally because the bulbs are identical. Find the total resistance first, then the current. · Two bulbs are connected in parallel across a six volt supply. Each has resistance three ohms. Find the current in each branch and the total current from the supply. · Hint: Each branch sits directly across the supply, so each branch has the full six volts. Work out one branch first. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 18 marks. · Explain why adding a second identical bulb in parallel does not make the first bulb dimmer, while adding it in series does. · 4 marks · A twelve volt supply is connected to a series combination of a four ohm resistor and an eight ohm resistor. Find the current and the potential difference across each resistor. · 4 marks · A 12 V supply is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. Answer all three parts, showing the calculation for each. · 6 marks · (a) Calculate the current through the resistor. Give your answer in A. [2] · Working: Show the calculation you used · Unit: A · (b) The current is changed to 0.50 A. Calculate the potential difference across the same resistor. Give your answer in V. [2] · Working: Show the calculation you used · Unit: V · (c) The 3 A current flows for 20 s. Calculate the charge transferred. Give your answer in C. [2] · Working: Show the calculation you used · Unit: C · Match each circuit component to its position in the drawing. · 4 marks · A · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · A rectangular circuit. A battery is drawn on the left wire, a resistor on the top wire, and an ammeter marked A on the right wire. Numbered positions mark the battery, resistor, ammeter and a connecting wire. · Labels: A. Resistor: the component that opposes the current · B. Connecting wire: the path that carries charge around the circuit · C. Battery: the component that provides the potential difference · D. Ammeter: the meter that measures current · Write the letter of the correct label beside each numbered position. · 1. ____________ · 2. ____________ · 3. ____________ · 4. ____________ · Use it in a new situation · A car has two identical headlight bulbs. With both connected, the battery supplies more current than with one. A student says this proves the second bulb is using extra energy that the first no longer gets. Use the parallel rules to explain what is actually happening and why the first bulb is unaffected. · The setting is a vehicle rather than a drawn circuit, and the wrong explanation is plausible because the total current really does rise. The learner has to separate the branch quantity from the supply quantity, which is the same reasoning in a context with no diagram. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · A two ohm and a six ohm resistor are in parallel across a twelve volt supply. What is the current in each branch? (next day) · Explain, in terms of energy per coulomb, what a voltmeter reading of six volts across a bulb means. (week later) · A filament bulb's current-voltage graph curves upward. What does that tell you about its resistance as it heats, and which assumption in V = I R has stopped holding? (month later) · Summary · Charge is conserved and flows; energy per charge is transferred. Current and potential difference are those two ideas measured. · In series the current is the same everywhere and the potential differences add; in parallel the potential difference is the same across each branch and the currents add. · V = I R holds for a component at constant temperature, and the unit is part of the answer. · Brightness follows the energy transferred per coulomb, which is the potential difference across the bulb. · OpenMind-authored lesson.
