documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · What is code? · computing · GCSE Computer Science, programming: sequence, selection and iteration · Key Stage 3 to GCSE · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Read a short program and predict its output without running it. · You will show this by: Given a loop that adds the numbers one to five, the learner states that the output is fifteen and can point to the line where the running total changes. · Trace a program's variables one line at a time and record their values. · You will show this by: The learner produces a table whose rows are the loop iterations and whose columns are the loop variable and the running total, and the final row matches the printed output. · Find a fault in a program by comparing the trace with the intended behaviour, and repair it. · You will show this by: Given a loop that starts at zero or stops one iteration early, the learner names the line, states what it should be, and explains why the change fixes the output. · Before you start · A recipe says: crack two eggs, whisk, then pour into a pan. Does the order matter? · What is a variable in mathematics? · Why this matters · A calculator has no idea what a number is. Press the buttons in one order and you get an answer; press the same buttons in another order and you get a different one. The machine did exactly what it was told both times. · Code is a list of instructions a computer follows exactly, in order, without judgement. That is why a program can be wrong while running perfectly: the computer has no idea what you meant. Learning to read code is learning to predict what the machine will do, which is the only reliable way to find out why it did something else. · The explanation · A program is a sequence of instructions · Code is written as a list of statements, and the computer executes them one after another, top to bottom, unless a statement changes the order. Each statement does one small thing: stores a value, adds two numbers, compares two values, prints something. Nothing happens by implication — if the program does not say it, it does not happen. · That is why the same instructions in a different order produce a different result. It is also why a program that runs is not necessarily correct: the computer will faithfully execute a wrong instruction. · Variables are named boxes · A variable is a name for a stored value. Writing total = 0 puts zero in a box labelled total. Later, total = total + 5 reads the value in the box, adds five, and puts the new value back in the same box. The equals sign here is not a mathematical claim that both sides are equal; it is an instruction to store. · Understanding that distinction is what makes a trace possible. After total = total + 5 you can say exactly what is in the box, and that is the state of the program at that moment. · Selection and iteration change which lines run · An if statement runs a block only when a condition is true. A for loop runs a block once for each value in a sequence. Between them they are why a program can be short and still do a great deal of work. · A for loop is not a vague repetition. It names a variable, gives it each value in turn, and runs the body once per value. Knowing how many times the body runs is the difference between predicting the output and guessing it. · A trace is how you find out what a program actually did · A trace is a table with one row per iteration and one column per variable that changes. Fill it in by hand, following the program line by line. At the end, the last row tells you the values the program finished with, which is what the output must be. · Tracing is also the debugging method. If the intended answer is fifteen and the trace ends at ten, the difference is not a mystery: the last iteration did not run, or the running total started in the wrong place. The trace localises the fault to a line, which a guess cannot do. · Diagrams and representations · A program that adds the numbers from one to five. Read it as five instructions plus a loop, not as a sentence. · total = 0 · for n in range(1, 6): ·     total = total + n · print(total) · The loop variable n takes the values one, two, three, four and five. The running total is updated once per value, and the print happens after the loop. · The trace of the program above. Each row is one pass through the loop; the last row is the state when the loop ends. · n = 1  total = 1 · n = 2  total = 3 · n = 3  total = 6 · n = 4  total = 10 · n = 5  total = 15 · The total after the final iteration is fifteen, so that is what the program prints. If your prediction is different, the disagreement is in one of these five rows. · Three tests for a program that is meant to add the numbers from one to n. One normal case, one boundary case and one invalid case, because a program that works for five may fail at zero. · n = 5 → 15 · n = 1 → 1 · n = 0 → 0 · The boundary case is the one that catches a loop written as range(1, n) instead of range(1, n + 1): it returns zero for n equal to one. · A faulty version of the same program. The loop stops one value early, so the last addition never happens. · total = 0 · for n in range(1, 5): ·     total = total + n · print(total) · The output is ten rather than fifteen. The fault is the upper bound of the range, not the addition and not the print. · Worked examples · Predict the output of this program without running it: total = 0 for n in range(1, 6): total = total + n print(total) · Work out how many times the loop body runs: range(1, 6) gives one, two, three, four and five, so five times. · Why: The upper bound in a range is exclusive in Python. Reading it as inclusive gives four iterations and a wrong total, which is the most common prediction error in this shape. · Trace the running total: after one it is one, after two it is three, after three it is six, after four it is ten, after five it is fifteen. · Why: Each iteration adds the current loop value to what is already in the box. Writing the intermediate values down is what makes the final answer checkable rather than remembered. · Read the print statement: it is outside the loop, so it prints once, after the last iteration, giving fifteen. · Why: Indentation decides which lines are inside the loop. A print inside the loop would print five times, once per iteration. · Answer: The program prints 15. · This program is meant to add the numbers from one to five but prints ten. Find the fault and repair it: total = 0 for n in range(1, 5): total = total + n print(total) · Trace the program as written: n takes one to four, giving totals one, three, six and ten. · Why: A trace turns 'it is wrong' into 'it stops after four'. Debugging starts from what the program did, not from what it was meant to do. · Compare the trace with the intended behaviour: the addition is correct and the print is correct, but the last iteration is missing. · Why: Two of the three parts of the program behave correctly, which narrows the fault to the loop bound. Changing the addition would break a part that already works. · Repair the range to range(1, 6), then re-trace: the final total is fifteen, which is the intended output. · Why: An exclusive upper bound must be one more than the last value you want. Re-tracing confirms the repair rather than assuming it. · Answer: Change range(1, 5) to range(1, 6). The output becomes 15. · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: The computer understands what you meant, so small mistakes in the code will be worked out. · Why it fails: A computer executes exactly the instructions it is given. There is no step that checks intent. A loop that runs four times instead of five is not a rough approximation of the intended program; it is a different program that happens to look similar. · Correct reasoning: Read the program as written, not as intended. If the code does not say it, it does not happen — which is what makes a trace more reliable than intuition. · Wrong: it obviously means one to five, so the computer will add all five · Right: range(1, 5) stops at four, so the computer adds four numbers · Wrong belief: A program that runs without an error message is correct. · Why it fails: An error message only reports that the program could not run. A program that produces the wrong answer runs perfectly. Ten is a perfectly valid output of the faulty loop, and the computer has no way to know that fifteen was wanted. · Correct reasoning: Correctness is tested against expected outputs, not against the absence of crashes. Test a normal case, a boundary case and an invalid case. · Wrong: no error, so it works · Right: it runs and prints 10, but the test says 15, so it is wrong · Wrong belief: The equals sign in total = total + 5 is a mathematical equation. · Why it fails: Read as an equation, total would have to equal itself plus five, which is impossible. The statement is not a claim about equality; it is an instruction to evaluate the right-hand side and store the result in the named box. · Correct reasoning: Read assignment as 'becomes'. The right-hand side is calculated first using the current value, and the result replaces what was in the variable. · Wrong: total = total + 5 is impossible, so nothing changes · Right: total becomes its old value plus five · Guided practice · How many times does the body of this loop run? for i in range(0, 4): print(i) · Hint: List the values range(0, 4) produces before counting them. · Trace this program and state its output: total = 1 for n in range(1, 4): total = total + n print(total) · Hint: Start from one, and add each of one, two and three in turn. · This loop is meant to print the numbers 1 to 5 but prints 1 to 4. What single change fixes it? for i in range(1, 5): print(i) · Hint: Decide which value is missing, then ask what the upper bound must be to include it. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 16 marks. · Write a program that prints the total of the even numbers from 2 to 10 inclusive. Then give the trace of the running total for at least two iterations, and state the output. · 4 marks · total = 0 · for n in range(2, 10, 2): ·     total = total + n · print(total) · Checks: the total includes 10 · Line / step	Value or output · 1	 · 2	 · 3	 · 4	 · Explain why a program can run without any error message and still be wrong. Use an example from a loop in your answer. · 4 marks · Put the steps of this total-finding algorithm in the order a program runs them. Use Up and Down; no dragging is required. · 4 marks · Set the running total to 0. order ____ · Print the running total. order ____ · For each even number from 2 to 10, repeat the next step. order ____ · Add the current number to the running total. order ____ · Match each programming idea to the behaviour it describes. · 4 marks · Programming idea	Answer letter	Behaviour · 1. Sequence		A. A condition chooses which path runs · 2. Selection		B. Statements execute in the order written · 3. Iteration		C. Named storage whose value can change · 4. Variable		D. A block of statements repeats · 5. Trace		E. A record of values at each step · Use it in a new situation · A vending machine program is meant to refuse a purchase when the credit is less than the price. It currently allows a purchase when the credit exactly equals the price minus one penny. Describe how you would find the fault using a trace, and what kind of test would have caught it before release. · The setting is a state machine rather than a counting loop, and the fault is a boundary comparison rather than a range bound. The method — trace the state, compare with intended behaviour, test the boundary — is the same one the lesson taught. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · What does range(1, 4) produce, and how many times does a loop over it run? (next day) · Explain the difference between `total = total + 1` and `total == total + 1`. (week later) · A loop is meant to run five times but runs four. What are the two most likely causes, and how would a trace distinguish them? (month later) · Summary · A program is a sequence of instructions executed exactly, in order. · A variable is a named box, and the equals sign stores rather than claims equality. · A loop's iteration count follows from the values it is given, not from the number written at the end. · A trace turns a wrong output into a named line, which is what makes debugging possible. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Correlation & regression basics · maths · GCSE Mathematics, statistics: scatter graphs, positive and negative correlation, lines of best fit, interpolation, extrapolation and the distinction between correlation and causation · Key Stage 3 to GCSE Foundation and Higher · version 1.1.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Describe a scatter graph by the direction and strength of its correlation, using the pattern rather than a single pair of points. · You will show this by: The learner identifies a rising cloud as positive correlation, a falling cloud as negative, and a formless cloud as no correlation, and explains that strength is about how closely the points follow the pattern. · Draw or use a line of best fit and calculate its equation from two points on the line. · You will show this by: The learner uses points (2, 58) and (6, 78) to obtain gradient 5 and equation y = 5x + 48, and predicts y = 70.5 at x = 4.5. · Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation and state why a prediction outside the data range is less reliable. · You will show this by: The learner predicts inside the observed x-range with confidence, and refuses to treat a prediction at x = 12 as equally trustworthy because the line has not been tested there. · Explain why correlation does not establish causation, naming a plausible third factor or reverse causation. · You will show this by: The learner explains that ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together because hot weather drives both, and does not conclude that buying ice cream causes drowning. · Explain how an outlier can change a line of best fit and a correlation judgment. · You will show this by: The learner describes an outlier pulling the line toward it and weakening or reversing the apparent pattern, and says the original data should be checked before the point is discarded. · Before you start · Which chart is appropriate for two measured variables on the same individual? · Find the gradient of the line through (2, 4) and (6, 12). · A line has equation y = 3x + 1. What is y when x = 4? · What does a negative gradient mean on a graph? · Why this matters · A café records the outdoor temperature and its hot-drink sales for ten days. On a scatter graph, the points tend to fall as temperature rises: hotter days, fewer hot drinks. That is negative correlation. A second graph of hours studied against test score tends to rise: positive correlation. A third graph of shoe size against test score is a formless cloud: no useful correlation. The direction and the tightness of the cloud are the first things to read. The second thing is what the pattern does not say: none of these graphs, by itself, proves that one variable causes the other. · Scatter graphs are how data with two measurements is inspected before a model is fitted. They appear in science practicals, economics, public health and machine learning. The line of best fit is a summary, and a summary is only useful inside the range and conditions it was made from. Interpolation is a reading inside that range; extrapolation is a claim beyond it. Correlation is a description of how two variables move together; causation is a claim about mechanism, which needs a controlled comparison or a credible explanation, not a sloping cloud. · The explanation · One point is one individual, with two measurements · A scatter graph plots one point for each individual or trial. The horizontal axis holds one measured variable and the vertical axis holds the other. Unlike a bar chart, neither axis is a category; unlike a line graph, the points are not joined in time order. The order of the points does not matter, and joining them would invent a sequence the data does not have. · Label both axes with the variable and its unit. The scales should be uniform and chosen so the pattern is visible without distorting it. A point's position is a pair of measurements, not an answer to a question; the pair is read together with every other pair. A single point far from the rest is an outlier, and it deserves a check before it is interpreted. · The pattern is a property of the cloud, not of any two points. Two points always define a line, so choosing a convenient pair can make almost any slope look convincing. Read the whole cloud first, then fit a line through its middle. · Direction: positive, negative or none · Positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to increase. Hours studied and test score usually show this. Negative correlation means that as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease; temperature and hot-drink sales usually show this. No correlation means the points form no clear upward or downward pattern. · Direction is not the same as steepness. A shallow rising cloud is still positive correlation; a steep falling cloud is still negative. The sign of the relationship is about which way the pattern runs, while the strength is about how closely the points cluster around it. · A correlation can be strong or weak. Strong correlation means the points lie close to a clear line or curve; weak correlation means the pattern is visible but loose. A single outlier can make a strong pattern look weak, or a weak pattern look strong, which is why the point is inspected rather than automatically deleted. · A line of best fit summarises the middle of the cloud · A line of best fit is a straight line through the middle of the points, chosen so that the vertical distances of the points above and below it are balanced. It does not have to pass through any particular point, and it should not be forced through the origin unless the context requires it. It is a model of the trend, not a join-the-dots path. · For a roughly linear cloud, take two points on the line — not necessarily data points — and calculate its equation. If the line passes through (2, 58) and (6, 78), the gradient is (78 − 58) ÷ (6 − 2) = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Using y = mx + c at (2, 58): 58 = 5 × 2 + c, so c = 48. The line is y = 5x + 48. · The equation turns a reading into a prediction. At x = 4.5, y = 5 × 4.5 + 48 = 70.5. The prediction is an estimate from the model, not a measurement. Report it with the same care as the data: a test score cannot be 70.5 marks if marks are whole numbers, and the context may require rounding. · Interpolation is inside the data; extrapolation is beyond it · Interpolation means predicting within the range of x-values that were observed. If the data run from x = 1 to x = 7, a prediction at x = 4.5 is interpolation. The line has support from points on both sides, so the estimate is reasonably trustworthy, though still an estimate. · Extrapolation means predicting outside the observed range. A prediction at x = 12 from data ending at x = 7 is extrapolation. The straight-line pattern may not continue: the relationship may curve, flatten or break down. In a test-score context, a prediction above 100 is impossible, which is an immediate signal that the model has left its valid range. · The distinction is about the data range, not the distance from the mean. A small extrapolation is still extrapolation. If a question asks for a prediction, state whether it is inside or outside the observed range and give the reason for your confidence. A number without that qualification hides the model's main limitation. · Outliers can pull the line and change the story · An outlier is a point that does not follow the overall pattern. It may be a recording error, a different population, or a genuine unusual case. Before deciding, check the original measurements and the context. Deleting a point merely because it weakens the preferred conclusion is not analysis. · A line of best fit is influenced by every point, so an outlier can tilt it toward itself. In a rising cloud, a low outlier at a high x-value pulls the right end of the line down, reducing the gradient. The line may then pass below the main cluster and give poor predictions for ordinary points. · An outlier can also create the appearance of correlation where none exists, especially in a small data set. Report the outlier, show the line with and without it if the decision matters, and explain which version is more defensible for the question. The goal is not a tidy graph; it is an honest summary. · Correlation is not causation · A correlation says the variables move together. It does not say which one drives the other, or whether a third variable drives both. Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together across the year, but buying ice cream does not cause drowning. Hot weather increases both: more people buy ice cream and more people swim. · Three common alternatives to a direct causal link are a common cause, reverse causation and chance. A common cause explains both variables at once, as temperature does. Reverse causation means the proposed effect is actually influencing the proposed cause. Chance means the pattern may be a coincidence in a small sample, which is why the size and selection of the data matter. · A controlled experiment, or a credible mechanism supported by other evidence, is needed before a causal claim. A scatter graph can suggest a hypothesis; it cannot confirm one. The correct sentence is 'the data show a positive association between x and y', not 'x causes y', unless the study design supports the stronger claim. · Reading a correlation claim critically · Ask what was measured, on whom, and over what range. A correlation computed over a narrow range can be strong without saying much outside it. A correlation in a selected group may not hold in the wider population. A correlation based on averages can differ from one based on individuals, sometimes reversing sign entirely. · Ask how the variables were defined. Changing the units does not change the correlation, but changing the definition can. Ask whether the relationship is linear; a strong curved relationship can have a modest straight-line correlation, and a straight line can be a poor summary even when the correlation is high. · Finally, separate the numerical summary from the causal story. A correlation coefficient near 1 or −1 describes a tight linear pattern; it does not describe a mechanism. The graph and the coefficient are evidence about association, and the causal claim needs its own evidence. · Diagrams and representations · 40 · 50 · 60 · 70 · 80 · 90 · 0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · 8 · Hours studied · Test score · Seven dots plot hours studied against test score. The cloud rises from left to right and lies fairly close to a straight pattern, so the correlation is strong and positive. The dashed line is the fitted line y = 5x + 48, passing through (2, 58) and (6, 78); it summarises the middle of the cloud rather than joining the points in order. · Each point pairs one individual's two measurements. The cloud's direction and tightness describe the correlation. · hours studied x: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7   ·   test score y: 52, 58, 61, 68, 72, 79, 83 · The table above gives the seven paired measurements; the drawing plots each pair as one point without joining the points in row order. · A line of best fit through the middle of the cloud can be written as an equation and used for predictions. · through (2, 58) and (6, 78): gradient = (78 − 58)/(6 − 2) = 5   ·   y = 5x + 48   ·   at x = 4.5, y = 70.5 · The gradient is the change in the predicted score per extra hour. The intercept is the model's value at x = 0, which may or may not be meaningful in context. · Interpolation stays inside the observed x-range; extrapolation goes beyond it and relies on the pattern continuing. · observed x: 1 to 7   ·   x = 4.5 is interpolation   ·   x = 12 is extrapolation · A prediction at x = 12 from data ending at x = 7 is a claim about the model, not a reading from the data. The straight line may not continue. · A correlation can have a common cause, reverse causation or chance behind it. The graph alone does not choose between them. · ice-cream sales ↑ and drowning deaths ↑   ·   common cause: hot weather   ·   not: ice cream causes drowning · The association is real; the causal direction is not established by the scatter graph. A controlled comparison or a plausible mechanism is needed. · Worked examples · A scatter graph plots hours studied against test score. The points rise from about (1, 52) to (7, 83) and lie fairly close to a straight line. Describe the correlation and explain what the pattern does and does not show. · Read the direction first: as hours studied increases from 1 to 7, the test scores tend to increase from about 52 to about 83. · Why: The overall movement from left to right describes the sign of the relationship. One pair of points is not enough; the pattern across the cloud is what matters. · Read the strength: the points lie fairly close to a line, so the positive correlation is strong rather than weak. · Why: Strength is about how tightly the points cluster around the trend. A rising cloud with wide scatter would still be positive but weaker. · State the association without claiming a cause: more study time is associated with higher scores, but the graph does not prove that studying caused the increase. · Why: Other variables, such as prior attainment or motivation, could influence both. A correlation describes co-movement, not a mechanism. · The correlation is strong and positive: as study time rises by 1 hour, the score tends to rise by about 5 marks. The graph shows an association, not proof that studying causes the higher score. · Why: The approximate rate comes from the overall slope, not from a single pair. The final clause keeps the causal claim separate from the numerical description. · Answer: strong positive correlation; about 5 marks per extra hour, but not proof of causation · A line of best fit passes through (2, 58) and (6, 78). Find its equation and predict the score at 4.5 hours. · Find the gradient: change in y ÷ change in x = (78 − 58) ÷ (6 − 2) = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. · Why: The gradient is the predicted change in the vertical variable for each one-unit increase in the horizontal variable. · Use y = mx + c with one point: 58 = 5 × 2 + c, so c = 58 − 10 = 48. The equation is y = 5x + 48. · Why: Substituting a point on the line fixes the intercept. Using a point not on the line would give a different, wrong intercept. · Substitute x = 4.5: y = 5 × 4.5 + 48 = 22.5 + 48 = 70.5. · Why: The prediction is inside the observed range 1 to 7, so it is interpolation. It is still an estimate from the model, not a measurement. · The equation is y = 5x + 48, and the predicted score at 4.5 hours is 70.5. The prediction is interpolation because 4.5 lies inside the data range 1 to 7. · Why: Naming the range separates a supported estimate from an extrapolation. It also tells the reader why this prediction is more defensible than one at x = 12. · Answer: y = 5x + 48; predicted score 70.5 at 4.5 hours (interpolation) · The same line y = 5x + 48 is fitted to data with x from 1 to 7. Predict the score at 12 hours, and explain why the prediction should not be trusted. · Substitute x = 12: y = 5 × 12 + 48 = 60 + 48 = 108. · Why: The equation can be evaluated at any x. Arithmetic validity is not the same as contextual validity. · Compare 12 with the observed range 1 to 7: 12 is outside the range, so this is extrapolation. · Why: The line was fitted to data between 1 and 7. Outside that interval, there is no evidence that the same straight-line pattern continues. · Check the context: a test score of 108 is impossible if the maximum is 100, so the model has produced a value that cannot occur. · Why: A prediction that violates a known bound is a signal that the model is being used beyond its range. The arithmetic is correct; the application is not. · The predicted value is 108, but it is an extrapolation beyond the data range 1 to 7 and exceeds the possible score, so it should not be trusted. · Why: The final sentence gives both reasons: distance beyond the observed range and a context bound. Either one is enough to reject the prediction as a real forecast. · Answer: 108 at 12 hours; extrapolation beyond 1–7 and above the maximum score, so unreliable · A line y = 2x + 1 predicts y = 9 at x = 4. A new point is measured at (4, 15). Explain what the point is and how it could affect the line. · Compare the observed value 15 with the prediction 9 at the same x = 4. The point is 6 units above the line. · Why: A residual is the vertical distance between the observed point and the model's prediction. A large residual marks a point the model does not explain well. · The point (4, 15) is an outlier relative to the pattern summarised by y = 2x + 1. · Why: An outlier is a point that does not follow the overall pattern. It may be a genuine extreme case or a measurement error, so it should be checked before it is removed. · If the line is refitted with this point, it will be pulled upward at the right-hand end, which tends to increase the gradient and the intercept. · Why: A line of best fit balances all points. A high point at a large x-value exerts leverage on the right end, so the line tilts toward it. · The new point (4, 15) is an outlier 6 units above the prediction 9; refitting can tilt the line upward, so the original data and the reason for the point must be checked first. · Why: The explanation connects the residual to the line's leverage and then to the decision. Deleting the point without checking would hide a real observation or a real error. · Answer: outlier 6 units above the predicted 9; it can tilt the line upward, so check it before refitting · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: If two variables are correlated, one must cause the other. · Why it fails: Correlation describes co-movement, not mechanism. A third variable can drive both, the causal direction can be reversed, or the pattern can be chance. Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together because hot weather increases both, not because ice cream causes drowning. · Correct reasoning: State the association first, then ask what else could explain it. A causal claim needs a controlled comparison or a credible mechanism supported by evidence beyond the scatter graph. · Wrong: The graph rises, so studying causes higher scores · Right: The graph shows a positive association; a controlled study is needed before claiming that studying causes higher scores · Wrong belief: A line of best fit must pass through the first and last data points. · Why it fails: A line of best fit summarises the middle of the cloud. It need not pass through any data point, and forcing it through the extremes lets two unusual points control the whole model. The best line balances the vertical distances of all points. · Correct reasoning: Draw the line through the middle of the pattern, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below. Choose two points on the line itself to calculate its equation, not two data points that happen to be convenient. · Wrong: Join the lowest and highest points and call it the line of best fit · Right: Draw a line through the middle of the cloud; it may pass through no data point at all · Wrong belief: A prediction from the line is equally reliable anywhere the equation can be evaluated. · Why it fails: The line is supported only by the observed range. Outside that range the relationship may curve, flatten or break down, and context bounds may make the prediction impossible. A test score above 100 is the clearest example: the arithmetic works, but the answer cannot occur. · Correct reasoning: State whether the prediction is interpolation (inside the observed range) or extrapolation (outside it). Treat extrapolation as a cautious hypothesis, and check it against context bounds and any reason the pattern might change. · Wrong: The equation gives 108 at 12 hours, so the score will be 108 · Right: 108 is an extrapolation beyond the observed 1–7 hours and above the maximum score, so it is not a credible forecast · Wrong belief: A negative correlation means there is no relationship. · Why it fails: Negative correlation is a relationship in which one variable tends to fall as the other rises. It can be just as strong as a positive correlation. 'No correlation' is the formless cloud, not a falling one. · Correct reasoning: Read the direction from the slope of the cloud: rising is positive, falling is negative, formless is none. Strength is separate: a steep falling cloud can be a strong negative relationship. · Wrong: Hotter days mean fewer hot drinks, so there is no correlation · Right: Hotter days mean fewer hot drinks: that is a negative correlation · Wrong belief: An outlier should always be deleted because it spoils the pattern. · Why it fails: An outlier may be a recording error, a different population, or a genuine extreme case. Deleting it without checking can hide a real effect or a data-quality problem. It can also change the line and the correlation in ways that matter to the conclusion. · Correct reasoning: Check the original measurement and context first. If the point is valid, report the line with and without it and explain which is more appropriate. Never remove a point only because it weakens the desired story. · Wrong: Remove the low point so the rising line looks stronger · Right: Check the low point; if it is valid, show how it changes the line and discuss both fits · Wrong belief: A strong correlation means the line will predict every individual accurately. · Why it fails: A correlation describes the overall pattern, not each point. Even a strong correlation leaves scatter around the line, and an individual can be well above or below the prediction. The line predicts an average tendency, not a guarantee. · Correct reasoning: Report the prediction as an estimate with the scatter visible. Use the graph to see the spread around the line, and do not turn a group-level trend into a claim about one person. · Wrong: The correlation is strong, so this learner will score exactly 70.5 · Right: The line predicts about 70.5 on average; individual scores vary around it · Guided practice · A line of best fit passes through (2, 58) and (6, 78). Find its gradient. · Hint: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x. · Using the line y = 5x + 48, predict the score at 3 hours. · Hint: Substitute x = 3 into the equation. · The data range is x = 1 to x = 7. Is a prediction at x = 10 interpolation or extrapolation? · Hint: Compare 10 with the observed range. · A rising cloud has one point far below the line at a high x-value. What happens to the line of best fit if that point is included? · Hint: A line balances all points, so a low point at the right end pulls that end down. · As temperature rises, hot-drink sales fall. What type of correlation is this? · Hint: The variables move in opposite directions. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 27 marks. · A line of best fit passes through (1, 50) and (5, 70). Find its gradient. · 4 marks · A study finds a strong positive correlation between the number of firefighters at a fire and the amount of damage. Explain why it would be wrong to conclude that sending more firefighters causes more damage. Suggest a more plausible explanation and state what kind of evidence would support a causal claim. · 4 marks · A line of best fit has equation y = 4x + 10. Predict y when x = 6. · 4 marks · Explain what an outlier is and describe two different ways it can affect a line of best fit or a conclusion from a scatter graph. · 4 marks · A correlation coefficient of −0.9 is found between two variables. Describe the direction and strength of the correlation. · 4 marks · A line of best fit has equation y = 4x + 12. Answer both parts. Each part is worth 2 marks: one for the method you show and one for the final answer. · 4 marks · (a) Use the equation to predict y when x = 3. [2] · Working: Show the substitution into y = 4x + 12. · (b) The line predicts y = 40. Work out the value of x that gives this prediction. [2] · Working: Show how you rearrange the equation. · A café models hot-drink sales against outdoor temperature. Its line of best fit is y = −3x + 40, where x is temperature in °C and y is sales in cups. Give the line on the grid, then read a prediction from the line you have drawn. · 3 marks · (a) Give two points on the line y = −3x + 40. [2] · x · y · 0 · 0 · 5 · 25 · 10 · 50 · (b) Use your line to predict sales when the temperature is 4 °C. [1] · Use the graph you drew in part (a) at x = 4. · Use it in a new situation · A school finds that students who eat breakfast score higher on a test. The correlation is positive and moderate. A governor concludes that the school should provide breakfast to raise scores. Evaluate the conclusion. Propose one common-cause explanation, one reverse-causation explanation and one way to gather stronger evidence. · The learner must apply the correlation/causation distinction to a new context, generate competing explanations rather than only rejecting the causal claim, and propose a design that could distinguish them. The task also tests whether the learner can keep the observed association while rejecting an unsupported mechanism. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · A line passes through (2, 10) and (6, 30). Find its gradient. (next day) · Using y = 3x + 2, find y when x = 5. (week later) · What is the difference between correlation and causation? (week later) · Why is interpolation usually more reliable than extrapolation? (month later) · What effect can an outlier have on a line of best fit? (month later) · Summary · A scatter graph plots one point per individual, with one measured variable on each axis. · Positive correlation: both variables tend to rise together. Negative: one tends to fall as the other rises. None: no clear pattern. · Strength is how closely the points follow the pattern; it is separate from direction. · A line of best fit goes through the middle of the cloud and need not pass through any data point. · From two points on the line, gradient = change in y ÷ change in x, then solve for the intercept. · Interpolation is inside the observed range; extrapolation is outside it and depends on the pattern continuing. · An outlier can pull the line and change the correlation; check it before deciding what to do. · Correlation is not causation: a common cause, reverse causation or chance can produce an association. · Only a controlled comparison or a credible mechanism supports a causal claim; the scatter graph suggests, it does not prove. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · PRINTABLE LESSON · Addition · maths · GCSE Mathematics, number: addition and written methods · Key Stage 2 to Key Stage 3 · version 1.0.0 · draft · Name: ______________________________ · Class: ______________ · Date: ______________ · Learning objectives · Add two whole numbers with a written method that lines up place values, carrying a group of ten into the next column. · You will show this by: The learner works out 47 plus 25 as 72 and shows the ten ones exchanged for one ten, rather than writing a two-digit total inside a single column. · Say why addition gives the same total in either order, and use that to choose an easier order. · You will show this by: The learner reorders 198 plus 203 as 200 plus 201, or adds 2 to one number and takes 2 from the other, and states that the total is unchanged. · Check an addition by estimating first and by adding back. · You will show this by: The learner estimates 47 plus 25 as about 75, rejects an answer of 612 as impossible, and checks a subtraction by adding the parts. · Before you start · In 47, what is the 4 worth, and what is the 7 worth? · How many ones make one ten? · Why this matters · A stadium turnstile counts 47 people through one gate and 25 through another. Nobody adds the digits 4, 7, 2 and 5 and gets 18: the two queues are counted as amounts, forty-seven and twenty-five, and the total is seventy-two. · Adding is combining two amounts of the same kind. The written method is not a set of rules to memorise but a way of keeping the kinds apart: ones are added to ones and tens to tens, and when a column holds ten or more, ten of them are exchanged for one of the next column. That exchange is the only new idea in the whole method. · The explanation · You can only add things of the same kind · Adding forty-seven and twenty-five means putting two collections together: forty-seven objects and twenty-five more. The answer is a single collection, and to count it reliably the objects need to be gathered by kind, ones with ones and tens with tens. That is what the columns of a written sum do. They are not decoration; they are the instruction to add like with like. · This is why the numbers are written one above the other with the ones vertically aligned. If the 7 and the 5 were not in the same column, the additions would mix tens with ones, and the total would describe a quantity nobody has. Aligning by column is the whole reason the method gives a correct answer. · Carrying is an exchange, not a trick · In 47 plus 25, the ones column holds 7 and 5, which is 12 ones. Twelve ones is one ten and two ones, so the ten is exchanged for a single ten in the next column and two ones stay where they are. The small 1 written above the tens column is a record of that exchange, not a lucky charm: it says one ten has moved in from the column on the right. · Because it is an exchange, the amount never changes, only its form. Twelve ones and one ten plus two ones are the same quantity, written differently. A learner who can say that sentence can carry in any column and can also explain why the method stops being needed when the column total is below ten: there is nothing to exchange. · Order does not change the total, and that is useful · Putting the two collections together in the other order gives the same collection, so addition is commutative: forty-seven plus twenty-five and twenty-five plus forty-seven are both seventy-two. Grouping three numbers differently also leaves the total unchanged, which is why a long list can be added in whatever order is easiest without altering the answer. · That freedom is a calculation tool, not just a fact. Two hundred and three plus one hundred and ninety-eight is awkward column work, but it is two hundred plus two hundred and one, which is four hundred and one. Noticing a number that is close to a round one, and adjusting, is often faster and always easier to check than the written method. · Diagrams and representations · The written sum, with the exchange recorded above the tens column. · 47 + 25 = 72 · Seven ones and five ones make twelve ones: two stay in the ones column and one ten is carried into the tens column. · Base-ten blocks for both numbers: four tens and seven ones beside two tens and five ones. The seven loose ones and five loose ones make a new rod, with two cubes left over. · 4 tens + 7 ones  +  2 tens + 5 ones  =  7 tens + 2 ones · The picture is the exchange: ten unit cubes become one rod, which is why the carried one belongs in the tens column. · Adding twenty-five in two jumps, tens first and then ones. · 47 → 67 → 72 · Forty-seven plus twenty is sixty-seven, and plus five more is seventy-two. Jumps on the line show addition as movement, which is the mental method written down. · Worked examples · Work out 68 plus 27 using a written method. · Write the numbers one above the other, with the ones under the ones. · Why: The method only adds like with like if the columns line up. Aligning by column is what turns two numbers into two collections of the same kinds. · Add the ones: 8 and 7 make 15, so write 5 and carry one ten. · Why: Fifteen ones is one ten and five ones. Only five can stay in the ones column, and the ten has to be exchanged into the column where tens are counted. · Add the tens, including the carried ten: 6 and 2 and 1 make 9. · Why: The carried ten is a ten, so it belongs with the other tens. Leaving it out is the most common slip and loses ten from the answer. · Read the total as 95, and check it against a rough estimate. · Why: Seventy plus thirty is about a hundred, so ninety-five is the right size. An estimate cannot prove the answer, but it can reject one that is wildly wrong. · Answer: 95 · Work out 198 plus 203 without a written column method. · Notice that both numbers sit close to a round number. · Why: A number two away from two hundred can be adjusted in the head far more easily than it can be added column by column. Choosing the method is part of doing the sum. · Write 198 as 200 minus 2, and 203 as 200 plus 3. · Why: Both forms describe the same amounts. Writing them this way puts the round parts together and leaves only a small adjustment. · Add 200 and 200 to get 400, then take 2 and add 3, giving 401. · Why: The adjustments are opposites, so they partly cancel. Doing them after the round parts keeps the arithmetic small enough to trust without writing anything down. · Answer: 401 · Common mistakes — and why they fail · Wrong belief: Add each column and write the whole two-digit total in that column, so 47 plus 25 becomes 612. · Why it fails: Writing 12 in the ones column puts a ten where ones are counted, so the answer claims twelve ones and no tens. The total 612 is not merely untidy: it is a different quantity, because each column can hold only one digit and the rest has to be exchanged. · Correct reasoning: When a column reaches ten or more, keep one digit there and exchange each ten for one in the next column left. Twelve ones becomes two ones and one ten, and the ten is added with the tens. · Wrong: 47 + 25 = 612, with 12 written in the ones column · Right: 47 + 25 = 72, with 12 ones exchanged for one ten and two ones · Wrong belief: The carried ten is separate from the other tens and can be written beside the answer instead of added. · Why it fails: The carry is a ten that has joined the tens column, so it is part of that column's total. Recording it separately loses it from the sum: 68 plus 27 would be recorded as 85 rather than 95, and the missing ten is exactly the exchanged group. · Correct reasoning: Add the carried ten in the same step as the other tens. Writing it small above the column is a reminder of what is coming, not a place to leave it. · Wrong: 68 + 27 = 85, with the carried one noted but not added · Right: 68 + 27 = 95, with 6 and 2 and the carried 1 making 9 tens · Guided practice · Work out 36 plus 48. · Hint: Start with the ones column, then decide whether anything needs exchanging. · Estimate 397 plus 205, then say whether an answer of 6,020 is plausible. · Hint: Round both numbers to the nearest hundred before deciding. · Work out 199 plus 201 by adjusting a round number. · Hint: One number is one below two hundred and the other is one above. · Assessment · Answer every question. Show working where it earns marks. Total: 8 marks. · Work out 68 plus 27. · 4 marks · A learner works out 47 plus 25 and writes 612 as the answer. Explain what they have done and what the correct answer is, in a way that shows why the carry exists. · 4 marks · Use it in a new situation · A club's three collections hold 198, 205 and 197 badges. Work out the total in a way you could do without writing a column sum, and explain the adjustment you made. · The numbers are chosen so that three amounts sit either side of a round number, and the learner has to decide on a method before computing. Recognising when not to use the written method is the skill being tested. · Remember it later · These questions are for a later lesson, not today. · Work out 58 plus 36. (next day) · What is 199 plus 205? (week later) · Work out 276 plus 158, and say which columns needed an exchange. (month later) · Summary · Addition combines two amounts of the same kind, which is why the columns are aligned. · A column that reaches ten exchanges ten of its units for one of the column to its left. · The total is the same in any order or grouping, which makes some sums easier in the head. · Estimate first: an estimate cannot prove a total, but it can reject the wrong size. · OpenMind-authored lesson. documents.text: OPENMIND · TEACHER GUIDE · NOT FOR PUPILS · Fractions · maths · GCSE Mathematics, number: fractions · Key Stage 3 to Foundation GCSE · version 1.1.0 · review state: draft · Classroom condition: Shared devices. One device per group, rotated between pupils. · At a glance · Decide which of two fractions is larger and justify it by the size of the pieces, not the size of the numbers. — evidence: Given three eighths and two fifths, the learner writes that three eighths is smaller because fifteen fortieths is fewer than sixteen fortieths — or compares each with one half — rather than because eight is bigger than four. · Write an equivalent fraction and explain why its value has not changed. — evidence: The learner produces fifteen twentieths for three quarters and says that multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number renames the pieces without changing how much there is. · Place a fraction on a number line between zero and one and read its position as a size. — evidence: The learner puts five eighths to the right of one half and left of one, and says why it is nearer to one half than to one. · One device is available for each group, not for each pupil. Groups can rotate the device operator. A group answer is not one pupil's individual evidence. · Before the lesson · Print the pupil worksheet and this guide. Print the answer key separately; it is the marking copy. · Have the board and exercise books ready. No pupil device, projector or laboratory is assumed. · One device is available for each group, not for each pupil. · Board plan · Objective: Decide which of two fractions is larger and justify it by the size of the pieces, not the size of the numbers. · Which is larger, three eighths or two fifths? Show how you decide. · First move: Notice that the two fractions are cut into different sizes of piece: eighths and fifths, so the top numbers cannot be compared yet. · Leave the remaining moves blank until pupils supply the reason for each one. · Keep the key subject term visible for the whole lesson. · Suggested run of show — 40 minutes · Adapt the timings to the period you actually have. The order matters more than the minutes. · Min	Step	What the teacher does · 3	Prior knowledge	Ask the prior questions. Take three answers before revealing the expected answer; do not reteach the whole prerequisite. · 8	Explain	Use the explanation headings below. Pause after each paragraph and ask one pupil to restate the key sentence. · 8	Worked example	Reveal one step at a time. Ask why the step is allowed before showing the written reason. · 8	Guided practice and group task	Groups of three or four, one shared device. Roles rotate: reader, recorder, challenger, device operator. Agree the answer out loud before it is entered. The teacher records only what the teacher observed; a group answer is not an individual mastery claim. · 8	Independent assessment	Pupils answer independently. A group answer or a sampled oral answer is formative feedback, not individual mastery evidence. · 5	Exit ticket and close	Use the exit prompt below. Finish with the summary; ask one pupil to say what they will remember tomorrow. · Temporary groups for this lesson · Use the prior check or exit ticket to place pupils. These groups are temporary: move pupils after the exit ticket. Do not use school year, age or a permanent label to decide a group. · Group	Focus	Task	What to check · Foundational	Secure the step before the new idea	Which is larger, two thirds or three fifths? Show the common denominator you used. Start with the hint: The smallest number that both three and five divide into is fifteen. Convert both fractions to fifteenths before comparing.	The pupil can start the task with the hint and say which step the hint supplies. · Developing	Use the new idea without the hint	Write a fraction equivalent to three quarters with denominator twenty.	The pupil completes the task without the hint and can name the rule used. · Applying	Apply it independently	Explain why one eighth is smaller than one quarter, even though eight is larger than four.	The pupil answers independently; a group answer is not individual evidence. · Extending	Transfer it to an unfamiliar problem	Two classes of the same size sit the same test. Three fifths of Class A pass and five eighths of Class B pass. Which class had the larger share pass? Decide without turning either fraction into a percentage, and say how you know.	The pupil explains why the idea transfers, not only the answer. · Prior-knowledge check · Ask: A chocolate bar is cut into four equal pieces and you eat one. A second identical bar is cut into eight equal pieces and you eat one of those. Which piece was bigger, and why? · Expected answer: The quarter. Cutting the same bar into more pieces makes each piece smaller, so an eighth is half the size of a quarter. · Ask: What does twelve divided by three mean, in words? · Expected answer: Either how many groups of three fit into twelve, or how big each share is when twelve is split into three equal parts. Both answers are four. · Teacher explanation · Fractions count pieces of a declared size · In three quarters, the four declares that the whole was cut into four equal pieces, and the three says how many of them you have. Read it aloud that way — three pieces, each a quarter — and the notation stops being two numbers stacked on top of each other. The bar between them is not a minus sign and not a division you have forgotten to finish; it is the word of, as in three of the four equal pieces. · That reading immediately explains the fact that surprises almost everyone: one eighth is smaller than one quarter, even though eight is bigger than four. The bottom number is not how much you get. It is how many ways the whole was divided, so a larger bottom number means a smaller slice. If you cut the same cake into more pieces, each piece must be smaller — there is no way around it, because the cake did not grow. · The same amount can wear different names · One half, two quarters and three sixths are the same amount of the same whole. Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number doubles the count and halves the piece size at the same time, and those two changes cancel exactly. You are renaming the pieces, not changing the amount of cake. That is why an equivalent fraction is written with an equals sign rather than an arrow: the number has not moved. · This is the move that makes comparison possible. Two fractions cut into different sizes of piece cannot be compared by their top numbers, because three big pieces and two small pieces are not counts of the same thing. Give both fractions the same denominator — the same size of piece — and the top numbers become plain counts that can be compared directly. · A fraction is one number in a place on the line · Three quarters is not a calculation waiting to happen. It is a single number that sits between zero and one, closer to one than to zero. Once you can see it there, adding, comparing and scaling it are operations on a number rather than rules about two integers that happen to be written above and below a line. · The number line also gives you a check that needs no arithmetic at all. Compare each fraction with one half: a fraction whose top is less than half its bottom is below one half, and one whose top is more than half its bottom is above it. Three eighths is below one half because three is less than four; two fifths is below one half because two is less than two and a half. To decide between them you still need a common denominator, but the check tells you immediately when an answer is impossible. · Decimals and percentages are the same number in another notation · Three quarters is also nought point seven five and also seventy-five per cent. Nothing about the quantity changes when the notation does: a fraction, a decimal and a percentage are three ways of writing one position on the number line. A learner who knows where three quarters sits already knows most of what the next two topics teach, and a learner who does not will find percentages mysterious for a reason that has nothing to do with percentages. · Worked example on the board · Which is larger, three eighths or two fifths? Show how you decide. · Notice that the two fractions are cut into different sizes of piece: eighths and fifths, so the top numbers cannot be compared yet. · Why: Comparing three with two only works when both counts describe pieces of the same size. Here three eighths and two fifths are counts of different things. · Rewrite both with a common denominator of forty: three eighths becomes fifteen fortieths, and two fifths becomes sixteen fortieths. · Why: Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number renames the pieces without changing the amount, so each fraction keeps its value. Forty is the smallest number that both eight and five divide into. · Now compare the counts of fortieths: fifteen is fewer than sixteen, so three eighths is the smaller fraction. · Why: Once the pieces are the same size, the top number is a plain count and can be compared directly. Fifteen fortieths is less than sixteen fortieths. · Answer: three eighths is smaller than two fifths (15/40 against 16/40, so 3/8 < 2/5) · What to listen for · Likely wrong belief: One eighth is bigger than one quarter, because eight is bigger than four. · Why it fails: The bottom number counts the pieces, so a larger bottom number means each piece is smaller. Cutting the same bar into eight makes every piece half the size of the quarter you had before. The numbers on the bottom are describing the cut, not the amount. · Say instead: Read the bottom number as a size and the top as a count. One piece of a bar cut into eight is smaller than one piece of the same bar cut into four, because there are more pieces sharing the same whole. · Wrong: 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4 · Right: 1/8 < 1/4 because eighths are half the size of quarters · Likely wrong belief: Two fractions with different bottom numbers can be compared by looking at their top numbers. · Why it fails: The top number is a count of pieces, and a piece of one size is not the same as a piece of another. Two large slices and three small slices cannot be counted against each other until the slices are the same size. Comparing tops alone answers a different question from the one that was asked. · Say instead: Make the pieces the same size first, by finding a common denominator, and only then compare the counts. Alternatively compare each fraction with one half, which needs no conversion. · Wrong: 3/8 > 2/5 because 3 > 2 · Right: 3/8 < 2/5 because 15/40 < 16/40 · Likely wrong belief: Adding two fractions means adding the tops and adding the bottoms. · Why it fails: Adding the bottoms changes the size of every piece in the answer, so the sum is no longer made of the pieces you started with. One half plus one half would become two quarters, which is one half — but two halves are a whole. The arithmetic has described a different operation from the one intended. · Say instead: Add counts of pieces that are already the same size. If the denominators match, add only the tops. If they do not, convert to a common denominator first, then add the tops. · Wrong: 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/4 · Right: 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/2 = 1 · Let us do one together · Which is larger, two thirds or three fifths? The teacher cannot read every pupil's written answer during the lesson. Oral and response-card checks are valid formative evidence, not individual mastery records. · Before the lesson · Print the pupil worksheet and this guide. Print the answer key separately; it is the marking copy. · Have the board and exercise books ready. No pupil device, projector or laboratory is assumed. · There may be no device for each pupil or each group. · Board plan · Objective: Decide which of two fractions is larger and justify it by the size of the pieces, not the size of the numbers. · Which is larger, three eighths or two fifths? Show how you decide. · First move: Notice that the two fractions are cut into different sizes of piece: eighths and fifths, so the top numbers cannot be compared yet. · Leave the remaining moves blank until pupils supply the reason for each one. · Keep the key subject term visible for the whole lesson. · Suggested run of show — 40 minutes · Adapt the timings to the period you actually have. The order matters more than the minutes. · Min	Step	What the teacher does · 3	Prior knowledge	Ask the prior questions. Take three answers before revealing the expected answer; do not reteach the whole prerequisite. · 8	Explain	Use the explanation headings below. Pause after each paragraph and ask one pupil to restate the key sentence. · 8	Worked example	Reveal one step at a time. These groups are temporary: move pupils after the exit ticket. Do not use school year, age or a permanent label to decide a group. · Group	Focus	Task	What to check · Foundational	Secure the step before the new idea	Which is larger, two thirds or three fifths? Show the common denominator you used. Start with the hint: The smallest number that both three and five divide into is fifteen. Convert both fractions to fifteenths before comparing.	The pupil can start the task with the hint and say which step the hint supplies. · Developing	Use the new idea without the hint	Write a fraction equivalent to three quarters with denominator twenty. Three fifths of Class A pass and five eighths of Class B pass. Which class had the larger share pass? Decide without turning either fraction into a percentage, and say how you know.	The pupil explains why the idea transfers, not only the answer. · Prior-knowledge check · Ask: A chocolate bar is cut into four equal pieces and you eat one. A second identical bar is cut into eight equal pieces and you eat one of those. Which piece was bigger, and why? · Expected answer: The quarter. Cutting the same bar into more pieces makes each piece smaller, so an eighth is half the size of a quarter. · Ask: What does twelve divided by three mean, in words? · Expected answer: Either how many groups of three fit into twelve, or how big each share is when twelve is split into three equal parts. Both answers are four. · Teacher explanation · Fractions count pieces of a declared size · In three quarters, the four declares that the whole was cut into four equal pieces, and the three says how many of them you have. Read it aloud that way — three pieces, each a quarter — and the notation stops being two numbers stacked on top of each other. The bar between them is not a minus sign and not a division you have forgotten to finish; it is the word of, as in three of the four equal pieces. · That reading immediately explains the fact that surprises almost everyone: one eighth is smaller than one quarter, even though eight is bigger than four. The bottom number is not how much you get. It is how many ways the whole was divided, so a larger bottom number means a smaller slice. If you cut the same cake into more pieces, each piece must be smaller — there is no way around it, because the cake did not grow. · The same amount can wear different names · One half, two quarters and three sixths are the same amount of the same whole. Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number doubles the count and halves the piece size at the same time, and those two changes cancel exactly. You are renaming the pieces, not changing the amount of cake. That is why an equivalent fraction is written with an equals sign rather than an arrow: the number has not moved. · This is the move that makes comparison possible. Two fractions cut into different sizes of piece cannot be compared by their top numbers, because three big pieces and two small pieces are not counts of the same thing. Give both fractions the same denominator — the same size of piece — and the top numbers become plain counts that can be compared directly. · A fraction is one number in a place on the line · Three quarters is not a calculation waiting to happen. It is a single number that sits between zero and one, closer to one than to zero. Once you can see it there, adding, comparing and scaling it are operations on a number rather than rules about two integers that happen to be written above and below a line. · The number line also gives you a check that needs no arithmetic at all. Compare each fraction with one half: a fraction whose top is less than half its bottom is below one half, and one whose top is more than half its bottom is above it. Three eighths is below one half because three is less than four; two fifths is below one half because two is less than two and a half. Show the common denominator you used. · Model answer: two thirds is larger: 2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15 · Marking guidance: Hint given: The smallest number that both three and five divide into is fifteen. Convert both fractions to fifteenths before comparing. · Write a fraction equivalent to three quarters with denominator twenty. · Model answer: fifteen twentieths · Marking guidance: Hint given: Ask what four was multiplied by to reach twenty, then multiply the top by the same number. · Put five eighths, one half and nine sixteenths in order, smallest first. · Model answer: one half, then nine sixteenths, then five eighths · Marking guidance: Hint given: Sixteenths is a common denominator for all three. Convert each fraction before ordering. · Assessment · constructed-response · Model answer: The bottom number says how many equal pieces the whole was cut into, so it describes the size of each piece rather than how many you have. Cutting the same whole into eight pieces instead of four makes every piece half as large, so one eighth is half of one quarter. · Marking guidance: States that the denominator describes the number (or size) of the pieces, not the quantity taken. · Uses the same whole being cut into more pieces, so each piece must be smaller. · Concludes that one eighth is smaller than one quarter, consistent with the reasoning. · constructed-response · Model answer: Sam added the denominators, which changes the size of the pieces in the answer. Halves and halves are already the same size, so only the top numbers should be added: one plus one is two halves, which is one whole. The answer is one, not two quarters. · Marking guidance: Identifies that adding the denominators changed the size of the pieces. · States that fractions with the same denominator are added by adding the numerators only. · Gives the correct answer of one whole. · diagram · Model answer: Each of the four equal sections is one quarter. Three of them are shaded, so the shaded fraction is three quarters. The denominator is four because the whole was cut into four equal parts, while the numerator is three because three of those parts are shaded. · One equal part, which is one quarter of the bar → position 1 · The part that is not shaded, also one quarter → position 2 · The denominator: the whole cut into four equal parts → position 3 · The numerator: the number of shaded quarters → position 4 · Marking guidance: Recognises one equal section as one quarter of the whole. · Recognises the unshaded section as the remaining quarter. · Connects three shaded quarters with the fraction three quarters. · Connects the denominator four with the number of equal parts in the whole. · short-answer · Model answer: Three quarters · Marking guidance: Uses a common denominator of four: one half is two quarters. · Adds two quarters and one quarter to get three quarters, without adding the denominators. · Transfer challenge · Two classes of the same size sit the same test.
